cards.q: Where does the Quran say Jesus (as) died? (Inni mutawaffika)
cards.a: Allah promised Jesus four things in a fixed order: first “I will cause you to die” (mutawaffika), then “raise you to Myself”. The death comes before the raising, and the Prophet’s cousin Ibn Abbas (ra) explained mutawaffika as “I will cause you to die.”
cards.x:
The verse lists four promises: (1) death, (2) raising/exaltation, (3) clearing his name, (4) his followers being above the disbelievers until the Day of Judgement. Each was fulfilled in this order. If Jesus had not died yet, the first promise would still be pending while the later ones are already fulfilled.

Ibn Abbas (ra), called “Tarjuman al-Quran” (interpreter of the Quran), gave the meaning as death — and Imam Bukhari placed this in his Sahih.

cards.q: Falamma tawaffaytani — how does 5:118 prove Jesus died?
cards.a: On the Day of Judgement Jesus will say his followers went astray only after Allah “caused him to die” (tawaffaytani). Christians have already adopted the Trinity — so he must already have died. The Holy Prophet (sa) used the exact same words about his own death.
cards.x:
Jesus divides time into two parts only: (1) while he was among his people, (2) after his tawaffi. The corruption (worship of Jesus and Mary) happened in the second part. Since the Trinity already exists, the second part — after his death — has already begun.

If he were to return before Judgement Day and see Christians worshipping him, he could not say “I do not know what they did after me.”

cards.q: Qad khalat min qablihir rusul — all prophets before Muhammad (sa) died
cards.a: When the Holy Prophet (sa) passed away, Hazrat Abu Bakr (ra) recited 3:145 — “all messengers before him have passed away”. All the Companions accepted it; Umar (ra) sat down. This was the first consensus (ijma) of the Sahaba: no earlier prophet was alive.
cards.x: Umar (ra) was saying the Prophet (sa) had not died and would return. Abu Bakr’s argument only works if *every* previous messenger had died: if Jesus were alive in heaven, Umar could have replied “Then why not Muhammad (sa) too?” Nobody objected — so all the Companions agreed that Jesus had died.

cards.q: Jesus and his mother “used to eat food” (5:76)
cards.a: The Quran says Jesus and Mary “used to eat food” — past tense. Elsewhere it says Allah never made prophets bodies that do not eat. A body needs food to live; since “used to” shows he no longer eats, he no longer lives in a body.
cards.x:
The verse makes a simple point about the body. It mentions Jesus (as) and his mother Mary together and says “they both used to eat food”. The words “used to” (kana) describe something that was true in the past and is no longer true.

Everyone agrees that Mary has died, so she no longer eats. The same verb covers Jesus, so the same must apply to him. The Quran also says in 21:9 that Allah never gave prophets bodies that live without food. A living human body needs food; if Jesus no longer eats, he is not living in a body.

So the verse, read with 21:9, shows that Jesus has passed away like the other messengers mentioned at its start.

cards.q: No human before the Prophet (sa) was given an extended life (21:35)
cards.a: Allah tells the Holy Prophet (sa): “We granted no human being before you everlasting/extended life. If you die, will they live on?” If Jesus has been alive for 2,000 years, he would have been given what was denied even to the best of prophets.
cards.x:
This verse was addressed to the Holy Prophet (sa) himself: Allah granted no human being before him an everlasting or extended life, and if he dies, others will not live on for ever.

The argument has three steps. Jesus (as) was a human being (bashar). He came before the Holy Prophet (sa). The verse says no human before the Holy Prophet (sa) was given such a life. So Jesus is included.

If Jesus had been alive for two thousand years, he would have been given something that Allah denied even to the greatest of the prophets. That would contradict the verse, and it would also place Jesus above the Holy Prophet (sa).

cards.q: Prayer and Zakat “as long as I live” (19:32)
cards.a: Jesus says Allah enjoined on him Prayer and Zakat “as long as I live”. In heaven, to whom would he pay Zakat? Either he is not alive, or he is breaking a command — the first is the only answer.
cards.x:
In Surah Maryam, Jesus (as) says that Allah has enjoined on him Prayer and Zakat “as long as I live”. These duties last for his whole life.

Zakat is given to the poor and needy among people. If Jesus were alive in heaven, he would still be bound to pay Zakat — but there are no poor in heaven to receive it. Either he is alive and not fulfilling a command of Allah, which no Muslim would accept for a prophet, or his life on earth has ended and the duty ended with it.

The verse therefore fits only one conclusion: his life, and with it his duties, came to an end.

cards.q: Could any human ascend bodily to heaven? (17:94)
cards.a: The disbelievers demanded that the Holy Prophet (sa) climb up into heaven. Allah told him to answer: “Holy is my Lord! I am only a human messenger.” Bodily ascension is something a human messenger does not do — so it is not attributed to Jesus either.
cards.x: The answer “I am only a human” shows that going up bodily into the sky is against the way Allah has made humans. If Jesus had done it, the disbelievers would have replied: “Jesus did it — so you are less than him.” Also 7:26 (7:25): “Therein shall you live, and therein shall you die” — the earth is the place of human life.

cards.q: What does “Allah raised him to Himself” (rafa’ahullahu ilayhi) mean?
cards.a: Rafa’ ilallah means spiritual exaltation and nearness to Allah — the opposite of the “accursed” death his enemies wanted. Allah is not located in the sky, and every use of rafa’ for a person in the Quran and Hadith is about rank, not the body.
cards.x: The Jews wanted Jesus to die on the cross so that he would be “accursed of God” (Deuteronomy 21:23) — i.e. not raised to God. The Quran answers exactly that claim: he was not killed on the cross; Allah raised him (in honour). Also 3:56 says death comes before raising (see Inni mutawaffika).

cards.q: “They did not kill him nor crucify him” — so what happened?
cards.a: The Quran denies that Jesus died on the cross (wa ma salabuhu = they did not kill him by crucifixion), not that he was put on it. “Shubbiha lahum” = it was made to appear to them like a death. He was taken down alive, recovered, and migrated east to seek the lost tribes of Israel.
cards.x:
Verse 4:158 denies two things: that the Jews killed Jesus (as), and that they crucified him — meaning they did not bring about his death on the cross. It does not deny that he was put on the cross.

The words “shubbiha lahum” mean that the matter was made to appear to them like a death. He was taken down alive and recovered. The Quran then says (23:51) that Allah gave Jesus and his mother refuge on an elevated land of valleys and springs.

The Bible points the same way: Jesus gave the sign of Jonah, who went into the whale alive and came out alive. With Muslims, ask who the innocent man punished in his place would be — the Quran never mentions anyone.

cards.q: Where did Jesus go after the crucifixion? (Kashmir)
cards.a: Jesus said he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Ten of the twelve tribes had been scattered east. The Quran says Allah gave Jesus and his mother refuge on a high land of valleys and springs. The tomb of Yuz Asaf in Khanyar, Srinagar is identified as his grave.
cards.x:
After surviving the cross, Jesus (as) still had a mission. He said he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and that he had other sheep not of this fold. Ten of the twelve tribes of Israel had been scattered towards the east.

The Quran says (23:51) that Allah gave Jesus and his mother refuge on a high land with green valleys and running springs. This description fits Kashmir. The tomb of Yuz Asaf in Khanyar, Srinagar is identified as his grave.

So his journey east completes the picture: he did not go up to the sky, but went to find the lost tribes, as he himself had said. The full study is in Jesus in India by the Promised Messiah (as).

cards.a: The Holy Prophet (sa) told Fatima (ra) that Jesus son of Mary lived for 120 years. He was about 33 at the crucifixion — so he lived on for many years on earth and then died.

cards.q: Hadith: “If Moses and Jesus were alive, they would have to follow me”
cards.a: The Holy Prophet (sa) said that if Moses and Jesus were alive, they would have no option but to follow him. This places Jesus with Moses among those who are not alive.
cards.x:
The Holy Prophet (sa) said that if Moses and Jesus were alive, they would have no choice but to follow him. The saying is recorded by Ibn Kathir in his commentary and by other scholars.

The words “if they were alive” show that neither was alive at the time. Everyone agrees Moses (as) had died, and the Holy Prophet (sa) placed Jesus (as) in the same sentence and under the same condition.

This pairs well with the hadith of the Mi’raj in Bukhari: the Holy Prophet (sa) saw Jesus together with Yahya (as), who had died, among the souls of the prophets — not in a living body.

cards.q: Grammar rule: what does tawaffa mean when Allah is the subject?
cards.a: In the whole Quran, whenever Allah is the doer of tawaffa and a human the object, it means taking the soul: death — or sleep only where sleep or night is mentioned. There is no example of it meaning “lifting the body alive to heaven”.
cards.x:
The key word in 3:56 and 5:118 is tawaffa. The rule is this: in the whole Quran, whenever Allah is the one doing tawaffa and a human being is the object, it means taking the soul — that is, death. It means sleep only where sleep or night is mentioned, as in 39:43.

The same word is used for the Holy Prophet (sa) in 10:47 and in Yusuf’s prayer in 12:102 (“let me die in submission”). Nobody translates these as being lifted bodily to heaven.

So the meaning of mutawaffika for Jesus (as) must be the same: “I will cause you to die.” A polite challenge works well: ask for a single example where Allah does tawaffa of a person and it means taking the body to heaven.

cards.q: If Jesus died, how will he “come back”?
cards.a: Like Elijah: the Jews waited for Elijah to physically return from the sky; Jesus said John the Baptist was Elijah — one who came in his spirit and power. In the same way, “Ibn Maryam” in the Hadith is a title for someone from this Ummah — “your Imam from among you”.
cards.x:
People ask: if Jesus (as) died, how can the Hadith speak of him coming back? The Bible gives the answer. The Jews were waiting for Elijah to return physically from the sky. Jesus said John the Baptist was Elijah — someone who came “in the spirit and power” of Elijah.

The Hadith follows the same pattern. Bukhari says the son of Mary will descend and “he will be your Imam from among you” — one from this Ummah. Bukhari also describes the earlier Jesus as reddish with curly hair, and the coming Messiah as wheat-coloured with straight hair. Two descriptions mean two different people.

So “Ibn Maryam” in the Hadith is a title for a follower of the Holy Prophet (sa) who comes in the spirit of Jesus.

cards.a: The Promised Messiah (as) announced a reward of 1,000 rupees for anyone who could show tawaffa — with Allah as subject and a living being as object — meaning anything other than taking the soul. No one has claimed it.
cards.x: Opponents ask: “Where did you get the rule that tawaffa means death when Allah is the doer and a person the object?” Answer: it is not a made-up rule — the classical Arabic dictionaries define it exactly this way.

cards.q: “Those they call upon besides Allah are dead, not alive” (16:21–22)
cards.a: The Quran says that all whom people worship besides Allah are “dead, not living”. Jesus is the most worshipped of them (5:18 — “they say Allah is the Messiah son of Mary”). So the Quran declares him dead.
cards.x:
Verses 16:21–22 describe everyone whom people call upon besides Allah: they create nothing, they were themselves created, and they are “dead, not living”.

The question is simply: who is called upon and worshipped besides Allah more than anyone else? Jesus (as). The Quran itself mentions those who say “Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary” (5:18). So Jesus is included among those the verse describes as dead, not alive.

The verse does not blame Jesus for being worshipped; it states a fact about all such figures: they have died.

cards.q: “Therein shall you live and therein shall you die” — the earth (7:26)
cards.a: Allah told the children of Adam that the earth is where they will live, die and be raised from. This is a general law for every human — so Jesus cannot be living in the heavens.
cards.x:
When Adam and his descendants were placed on earth, Allah said: “Therein shall you live, and therein shall you die, and therefrom shall you be brought forth” (7:26). Other verses say the earth is a receptacle for the living and the dead (77:26–27), and an abode for mankind for a time (2:37).

This is a general law for every child of Adam. Human life, death and resurrection are tied to the earth. The Quran makes no exception for Jesus (as).

So the belief that he has been living in the heavens for two thousand years goes against this law. The simple question is: where does the Quran make an exception for him?

cards.q: Follow-up questions on “Prayer and Zakat as long as I live”
cards.a: If Jesus is alive in heaven, he is still bound to pray and pay Zakat (19:32). Ask: to whom does he pay Zakat? Which way does he face to pray? Is he in the world of deeds or the world of reward?
cards.x:
• If he would have no wealth in heaven, the verse should have said مَا دُمْتُ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ (“as long as I am on earth”), not “as long as I live”.
• Prayer: if he learned the Islamic prayer by revelation in heaven, the Shariah came to him, not only to the Holy Prophet (sa). At the Mi’raj, prayer had not yet been made obligatory, so he could not have learned it then.
• Either he is in dar al-‘amal (world of deeds) — then all duties apply — or in dar al-jaza’ (world of reward), which means barzakh or paradise, i.e. after death.

cards.q: “A Messenger who will come after me, named Ahmad” (61:7)
cards.a: Jesus foretold a messenger coming “after me” named Ahmad — Muslims apply it to the Holy Prophet (sa). If the same Jesus returns now, he would come after Ahmad, and the Prophet would no longer be “after” him. So the old Jesus does not return.
cards.x:
In 61:7 Jesus (as) gives glad tidings of a Messenger who will come “after me” (min ba’di), whose name will be Ahmad. Muslims apply this to the Holy Prophet (sa).

Now think of the order. If the same Jesus of Nazareth came back today, he would be coming after the Holy Prophet (sa). The Holy Prophet (sa) would then no longer be the one who came after Jesus; Jesus would have the last word.

The Quran’s words “after me” only stay true if the Israelite Jesus does not return. The promised Messiah must therefore be someone else, from this Ummah.

cards.q: On Judgement Day the false gods will say “we were unaware of your worship” (10:29–30)
cards.a: All who were worshipped besides Allah will say on the Day of Judgement that they were unaware of being worshipped. Jesus is among them. If he had come back to earth and seen Christians worshipping him, he could not say this.
cards.x:
On the Day of Judgement, those who were worshipped besides Allah will say that they were quite unaware of being worshipped (10:30).

Jesus (as) is the one most worshipped besides Allah. If he had come back to the earth before the Day of Judgement, he would have seen with his own eyes millions of Christians worshipping him. He could then not say “I was unaware of your worship”.

This matches 5:118, where Jesus says he was a witness over his people only while he was among them, and that after Allah caused him to die, Allah was the Watcher over them. Both verses show he does not return to see what his followers did.

cards.q: “If Jesus were alive he would have to follow me” — Mulla Ali Qari
cards.a: Mulla Ali Qari, explaining why Jesus will pray behind the Mahdi, quotes the Holy Prophet (sa): “If Jesus were alive, he would have no option but to follow me.”
cards.x:
Mulla Ali Qari is one of the most respected Hanafi scholars. In Sharh Fiqh al-Akbar, while explaining why Jesus will pray behind the Mahdi, he quotes the Holy Prophet (sa): “If Jesus were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me.”

The words “if he were alive” show that, at the time of the Holy Prophet (sa), Jesus (as) was not alive. A great Hanafi scholar recorded this without objection.

This is especially useful with Hanafi listeners, because it comes from their own scholar and not from an Ahmadi writer.

cards.q: Hadith: no living soul will remain after a hundred years
cards.a: The Holy Prophet (sa) said no living soul on earth that day would still be alive after a hundred years, and that Allah sends a wind at the head of every century that takes the soul of every believer. Jesus is a believer and a living soul.
cards.x:
Sahih Muslim records the Holy Prophet (sa) saying that no living soul on earth that day would still be alive after a hundred years. Al-Mustadrak adds that Allah sends a wind at the head of every hundred years that takes the soul of every believer.

Jesus (as) was a living soul and a believer. If he was alive on that day, the hadith says he would not still be alive a hundred years later. Making an exception for him has no basis in the words of the Holy Prophet (sa).

So both narrations support the Quranic verses that he has died.

cards.q: Hadith: Allah told Jesus to keep moving from place to place
cards.a: Allah revealed to Jesus: “Move from place to place so that you are not recognised and harmed.” This fits a life of migration after the crucifixion — not being lifted to the sky.
cards.x:
Kanz al-Ummal records that Allah revealed to Jesus (as): “Move from one place to another, lest you be recognised and harmed.”

This describes a life of travelling and migration on earth, not being lifted up to the sky. Someone in heaven has no need to hide from people or keep moving so as not to be recognised.

The narration fits what happened after the crucifixion: Jesus survived, left the land of his enemies and travelled east in search of the lost tribes of Israel. It pairs well with the card on Kashmir.

cards.q: What did early Muslim scholars say about Jesus’ death?
cards.a: Many classical authorities held that Jesus died or that his “coming” would be in another person: Imam Bukhari (via Ibn Abbas), Imam Malik, Ibn Arabi, Ibn Jarir, Imam Jubba’i, a statement of Hazrat Aisha (ra) on his age, and Imam Hasan’s (ra) sermon.
cards.x:
Belief in the death of Jesus (as) is not an Ahmadi invention. Many classical authorities held it or said his “coming” would be in another person.

Imam Bukhari recorded Ibn Abbas’s explanation of mutawaffika as “I will cause you to die.” Ibn Jarir al-Tabari quotes the view that Jesus has died. Imam Jubba’i said Allah caused the Messiah to die. Ibn Arabi wrote that his descent in the latter days would be through another body. Hazrat Aisha (ra) is reported to have said Jesus lived 120 years, and Imam Hasan (ra) said Hazrat Ali was martyred on the night Jesus’ soul was raised.

These quotations show that respected scholars across the centuries held the same view.

cards.q: The dead do not return to this world
cards.a: The Quran repeatedly says that those who have died do not come back to this world. So the coming Messiah cannot be the Jesus of Nazareth who died; he is one from this Ummah.
cards.x:
The Quran says many times that those who have died do not return to this world. A township that Allah destroyed will not return (21:96); the dead “never return to them” (36:32); and behind them is a barrier until the Day they are raised (23:101).

Once it is shown from the Quran that Jesus (as) died, this principle settles the question of his return. The dead do not come back before the Day of Resurrection.

So the “son of Mary” promised in the Hadith must be someone else — a person from this Ummah who comes in his spirit, as Elijah came in John the Baptist.

cards.q: What does “Khatam an-Nabiyyin” actually mean?
cards.a: Khatam (with fatha) means a seal or signet ring — the seal that authenticates and adorns. The Holy Prophet (sa) is the Seal of the Prophets: the most perfect of them, whose seal any future spiritual rank must carry. Classical scholars explain khatam as “the most beautiful of the prophets”, “their adornment”.
cards.x:
The word in 33:41 is khatam, with a fatha on the ta. In Arabic this means a seal or a signet ring: the seal that authenticates a document and the ring that adorns its wearer.

Classical scholars explained it this way. Imam Zurqani wrote that khatam means the best of the prophets in form and character, like a ring with which one adorns oneself. Tafsir Fath al-Bayan says the same.

The context matters too. The verse says Muhammad (sa) is not the father of any of your men — but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets. In other words, he has no physical sons, but he is the spiritual father whose seal every later spiritual rank must carry. Saying only “he is the last” would not answer the point about sons.

cards.q: Hazrat Aisha (ra): “Say Khatam an-Nabiyyin, but do not say there is no prophet after him”
cards.a: Hazrat Aisha (ra) instructed: “Say he is the Seal of the Prophets, but do not say there is no prophet after him.” Scholars explained this as referring to the coming of the Messiah, and that “la nabiyya ba’di” means no prophet who abrogates his Shariah.
cards.x:
Hazrat Aisha (ra) said: “Say he is the Seal of the Prophets, but do not say there is no prophet after him.” This is recorded by Suyuti in Al-Durr al-Manthur and in Takmila Majma’ Bihar al-Anwar.

She drew a clear line between the two statements. The first is the Quran’s own term. The second, if taken to mean no prophet of any kind, would go beyond it.

The author of Majma’ Bihar al-Anwar explained that her words look to the descent of Jesus, and that “no prophet after me” means no prophet who abrogates the Holy Prophet’s (sa) law. This is exactly the Ahmadi position, stated by the Mother of the Believers herself.

cards.q: Founder of Deoband (Qasim Nanotwi) on Khatam an-Nabiyyin
cards.a: Maulana Muhammad Qasim Nanotwi, founder of Darul Uloom Deoband, wrote that taking khatam to mean merely “the last in time” is the view of the common people; the people of understanding know there is no merit in merely coming last. He added that even if a prophet appeared after the Holy Prophet (sa), his khatamiyyat would not be affected.
cards.x:
Maulana Muhammad Qasim Nanotwi founded Darul Uloom Deoband. In Tahdhir al-Nas he wrote that taking khatam to mean only “last in time” is the view of ordinary people. People of understanding know there is no special merit in simply coming last.

He went further: even if a prophet were born after the time of the Holy Prophet (sa), there would still be no difference to the finality (khatamiyyat) of Muhammad (sa).

This is useful with Deobandi listeners because it comes from the founder of their own school. Keep the page numbers and edition ready, and a scan if possible, since the quotation is often disputed.

cards.q: What does “La nabiyya ba’di” (no prophet after me) mean?
cards.a: Great scholars explained it as: no prophet will come with a new law or from outside the Ummah. Ibn Arabi: only law-bearing prophethood ended — like the Prophet’s (sa) words “when this Kisra dies there will be no Kisra after him.” Mulla Ali Qari: no prophet who abrogates his religion and is not from his Ummah.
cards.x:
“La nabiyya ba’di” — there is no prophet after me — is often taken to close the door completely. Great scholars explained it differently.

Ibn Arabi wrote that what ended was prophethood with a law: no new law-giver and no new law. Mulla Ali Qari wrote that no prophet will come who abrogates the Holy Prophet’s (sa) religion and is not from his Ummah. Abdul Karim Jili said the same.

The Holy Prophet (sa) used the same style elsewhere: “When Kisra dies there will be no Kisra after him” — yet kings continued in Persia; the negation is of that particular kind of rule. Most Muslims also believe Jesus will come as a prophet after the Holy Prophet (sa), so the real question is only what kind of prophet can come.

cards.q: Quran: “Allah chooses messengers from angels and from men” (22:76)
cards.a: Allah says He chooses (yastafi — present/future tense) messengers from angels and from mankind. The Quran is a book for all time; the verb shows the choosing continues.
cards.x:
Verse 22:76 says: “Allah chooses Messengers from among angels and from among men.” The verb yastafi is in the present-future tense: Allah chooses, and goes on choosing.

The Quran is a book for all time, and this verse was revealed to the Holy Prophet (sa). Angels still bring Allah’s commands — no one says that part has ended. The same verb in the same sentence covers human messengers too.

The verse therefore speaks of a continuing practice of Allah, not of something that ended before the Quran was revealed.

cards.q: Quran: Allah will not leave believers without sending a chosen messenger (3:180)
cards.a: Allah will not leave the believers in their state until He separates the good from the bad, and for that He chooses (yajtabi) from His messengers whom He pleases — and tells believers to believe in His messengers.
cards.x:
Verse 3:180 is addressed to the Muslims. Allah says He will not leave the believers in their present state until He separates the bad from the good, and that for this He chooses (yajtabi) from His messengers whom He pleases. Then it says: “Believe then in Allah and His messengers.”

The verb is in the present-future tense, and the purpose — sifting the good from the bad among believers — is a continuing need.

Read the verse slowly and ask whom Allah chooses from His messengers for the believers. The verse is about the Muslim community, not earlier nations.

cards.q: Obeying Allah and the Messenger leads to the rank of prophets (4:70)
cards.a: Whoever obeys Allah and this Messenger will be among those Allah has blessed: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. Just as obedience can make one siddiq, shahid and salih, it can — by Allah’s grace — lead to prophethood in his subordination.
cards.x:
Verse 4:70 says that whoever obeys Allah and this Messenger shall be among those whom Allah has blessed: the prophets, the truthful (siddiqin), the martyrs and the righteous.

Everyone agrees that by obeying the Holy Prophet (sa) a Muslim can become truthful, a martyr or righteous. The same sentence lists the prophets first. If “with” (ma’a) meant only standing next to them, then no Muslim could actually become a siddiq or shahid either.

Imam Raghib, quoted in Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit, explained it as rank and reward: the prophet with the prophets, the truthful with the truthful, and so on. So obedience can lead, by Allah’s grace, to prophethood under the Holy Prophet (sa).

cards.q: “O children of Adam, if messengers come to you from among you…” (7:36)
cards.a: Addressed to all mankind in the Quran revealed to the Holy Prophet (sa): “If messengers come to you from among yourselves…, whoever fears God and reforms will have no fear.” The emphatic future form shows the possibility of messengers remains.
cards.x:
Verse 7:36 addresses all mankind: “O children of Adam! If Messengers come to you from among yourselves, rehearsing My Signs to you, then whoever fears God and does good, on them shall be no fear, nor shall they grieve.”

This verse is in the Quran revealed to the Holy Prophet (sa), the final Book. The verb ya’tiyannakum is an emphatic future form. It tells all the children of Adam how to respond if messengers come.

If no messenger of any kind could ever come again, this guidance would have no meaning. Ask: is this verse cancelled?

cards.q: The covenant of the prophets — also taken from the Holy Prophet (sa) (3:82, 33:8)
cards.a: Allah took a covenant from all prophets to believe in any messenger who comes confirming what is with them. The Quran says this covenant was also taken from the Holy Prophet (sa) — which would be pointless if no messenger could come after him.
cards.x:
Allah took a covenant from all the prophets that they would believe in and help any messenger who comes confirming what is with them (3:82). Imam Razi explains that this made it obligatory on all prophets to believe in every such messenger.

Verse 33:8 says this covenant was taken from the prophets — “and from you” (minka), the Holy Prophet (sa) — and from Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus.

A covenant to accept a coming messenger would be pointless if no messenger could ever come after the Holy Prophet (sa). The question is simple: why take the covenant from him if the door was shut?

cards.q: “Had Ibrahim lived, he would have been a truthful prophet”
cards.a: When the Holy Prophet’s (sa) son Ibrahim died, the Prophet said: had he lived, he would have been a truthful prophet. This was said AFTER 33:41 (Khatam an-Nabiyyin) was revealed — so the Prophet (sa) did not understand Khatam to make prophethood impossible.
cards.x:
When the Holy Prophet’s (sa) son Ibrahim died, he said: “Had he lived, he would have been a truthful prophet” (Sunan Ibn Majah).

The timing is the key. Surah al-Ahzab, with the verse of Khatam an-Nabiyyin, was revealed around 5 AH. Ibrahim died in 10 AH. So after the verse was revealed, the Holy Prophet (sa) himself spoke of the possibility of a prophet from among his own family. He did not understand khatam to make every kind of prophethood impossible.

Imam Nawawi rejected the narration, but Imam Shawkani replied that it is narrated from three Companions and that its meaning was simply not clear to Nawawi.

cards.q: “Today I have perfected your religion” (5:4) — does it end prophethood?
cards.a: No. Perfection of the religion (the law) is exactly why no NEW law-bearing prophet can come. But “completing My favour” does not mean ending favours: the Torah was also called “complete”, yet more revelation followed; and Allah’s favours include prophethood, truthfulness, martyrdom and righteousness.
cards.x:
Verse 5:4 says Allah has perfected the religion and completed His favour. Some take this to mean prophethood has ended. It means something more precise.

The perfection of the religion — the law — is exactly why no new law-bearing prophet can come. But completing a favour does not mean ending all favours. The Quran calls the Torah “complete” too (6:155), yet more revelation came after it. And 5:21 lists prophets among Allah’s favours to a people, along with others.

So the verse closes the door to a new law, not to Allah’s continuing blessings within the perfected religion.

cards.q: Hadith “I am the ‘Aqib, after whom there is no prophet”
cards.a: The phrase is reported via Sufyan b. ‘Uyaynah from al-Zuhri. Hadith critics say Sufyan did tadlis, made mistakes in some twenty narrations from al-Zuhri, and his memory deteriorated in his last years; al-Zuhri also occasionally did tadlis. So it cannot overrule the Quran and stronger hadith.
cards.x: Even if accepted, ‘Aqib (one who comes after) is understood with “la nabiyya ba’di” — no law-bearing prophet independent of him (see that card). See also the site card “Al Aqib?”.

cards.q: The “last brick” hadith
cards.a: The Prophet (sa) compared prophethood to a house completed by the last brick. This refers to the building of the SHARIAH, which the earlier prophets built step by step and which he completed. If it meant there was a gap in prophethood itself that he filled as “a brick”, it would lower his status — he is the one for whom the universe was made.
cards.x: Earlier prophets brought laws according to the needs of their time; the edifice of law was completed with him. A brick fills a hole — a prophet who is a follower and reflection of him adds no new brick to the law.

cards.q: Allah sent the Prophet (sa) after an interval (fatrah) so people could not say “no warner came” (5:20)
cards.a: The Quran says the Holy Prophet (sa) came after a long gap in messengers, so that people would not say “no bearer of glad tidings or warner came to us.” The same reasoning holds in an age of darkness: Allah does not leave people without guidance.
cards.x:
Verse 5:20 says the Holy Prophet (sa) came “after a break in the series of messengers”, so that people could not say no bearer of glad tidings or warner had come to them.

This shows a principle of Allah’s mercy: after a long period of darkness, He sends guidance so that no one is left without a warner.

The same principle applies in our age, when Muslims themselves describe the deep decline of the Ummah. If Allah sent a messenger after a gap so that no one could complain, is our age in any less need?

cards.q: What do Ahmadis actually believe about the finality of prophethood?
cards.a: Ahmadis believe the Holy Prophet (sa) is Khatam an-Nabiyyin, his law is final until the Day of Judgement, and no one can attain any spiritual rank except through following him. Like the moon reflects the sun, Allah raises reformers (mujaddids) and, in this age, the Promised Messiah — a prophet subordinate to him, from his Ummah, with no new law.
cards.x: Hazrat Mirza Bashir Ahmad (ra) wrote “Khatm-e-Nabuwwat ki Haqeeqat” (1953) to answer the allegation that Ahmadis deny the finality of the Holy Prophet (sa). He compares the Holy Prophet (sa) to the sun whose light will last until the Day of Judgement; in times of darkness Allah raises spiritual “moons” — khulafa, mujaddids, and the Promised Messiah — who shine only with his reflected light.

cards.q: Proof 1: His pure life before the claim (10:17)
cards.a: The Holy Prophet (sa) was told to say: “I have lived among you a whole lifetime before this — will you not understand?” A prophet’s blameless life before his claim is a proof of his truth. The Promised Messiah (as) challenged his opponents to point to any fault in his life before his claim; even his later bitter opponent Maulvi Muhammad Husain Batalvi had praised him highly.
cards.x: The Promised Messiah (as) wrote that before his claim he lived in obscurity in Qadian; people of the area knew him, and he invited anyone to bring a charge against his earlier life. Maulvi Muhammad Husain Batalvi’s review of Barahin-e-Ahmadiyya (Isha’at al-Sunnah) praised him as a defender of Islam with no equal in that age.

cards.q: Proof 2: A false claimant cannot survive 23 years (69:45–47)
cards.a: Allah says if the Prophet had falsely attributed any saying to Him, He would have seized him and cut his life-artery. The Holy Prophet (sa) lived 23 years after his first revelation. The Promised Messiah (as) lived more than 23 years after his claim of revelation — no fabricator has ever been given that.
cards.x: Sharh al-‘Aqa’id al-Nasafiyyah (with al-Nibras) notes that false claimants like Musaylimah and Aswad al-‘Ansi were either killed or repented, and their affair lasted only a few days. Ibn Jarir writes that Allah punishes a false claimant to revelation quickly. The Promised Messiah (as) offered 500 rupees (Arba’in) to anyone who could show a false claimant of revelation who survived 23 years after his claim.

cards.q: Proof 3: “We had high hopes in you before this” (11:63)
cards.a: When Salih (as) claimed prophethood, his people said: “O Salih, you were one in whom we placed great hopes before this.” Before a claim, people praise a prophet; after it, they call him a liar. The same happened with the Promised Messiah (as): scholars like Muhammad Husain Batalvi praised him, then turned against him after his claim.
cards.x:
When Salih (as) made his claim, his people said: “O Salih, you were one in whom we placed great hopes before this” (11:63). Before a claim, people praise a godly man; after it, they turn against him and call him a liar (54:26).

The same thing happened with the Promised Messiah (as). Before his claim, scholars such as Maulvi Muhammad Husain Batalvi praised him and his book Barahin-e-Ahmadiyya in strong words. After his claim, the same people opposed him.

This pattern is a mark of truthful claimants in the Quran. Show Batalvi’s praise first, then read 11:63.

cards.q: Proof 4: The challenge of eloquent Arabic (11:14)
cards.a: The Quran challenged its deniers to produce ten surahs like it. As a reflection of that miracle, the Promised Messiah (as) wrote books in eloquent Arabic — such as I’jaz al-Masih and I’jaz-e-Ahmadi — challenging scholars to produce the like within a set time, with rewards. None did.
cards.x: He clarified that this eloquence is a shadow (zill) of the Quran’s miracle, given in its service (Zarurat al-Imam). Opponents later listed alleged “mistakes” in I’jaz-e-Ahmadi; the Pocket Book answers these in detail.

cards.q: Proof 5: Liars do not wish for death — the principle of Mubahala (62:7–8)
cards.a: The Quran told those who claimed to be God’s friends: if you are truthful, wish for death — they never will, because of what they have done. The Promised Messiah (as) invited opposing scholars to Mubahala (mutual prayer for God’s judgement) and set out exact conditions; his opponents would not come forward.
cards.x:
Verses 62:7–8 told those who claimed to be the special friends of Allah: if you are truthful, wish for death. They would never wish for it, because of what they had done. Someone who knows he is lying will not call God’s judgement on himself.

The Promised Messiah (as) applied this principle. In Anjam-e-Atham he invited all opposing scholars to Mubahala — a mutual prayer asking God to judge between them — and set out clear conditions. He wrote that if each of them was not struck by a visible calamity within a year, he would consider himself a liar. His opponents did not come forward.

The Quran also records the Mubahala offered to the Christians of Najran (3:62).

cards.q: Proof 6: A reformer comes when corruption fills land and sea (30:42)
cards.a: Prophets are sent when corruption spreads everywhere and people have strayed. Muslim writers of the 19th–20th century themselves described Islam’s decline — the Quran “lifted away”, believed in name only. That was the time for the promised reformer.
cards.x:
Prophets and reformers are sent when corruption fills the land and sea (30:42) and people have fallen into clear error (62:3).

In the 19th and 20th centuries, Muslim writers themselves described the decline of Islam — that the Quran had been lifted away in practice and that Muslims were Muslim only in name. The Pocket Book quotes these descriptions.

If the Ummah was in such a state, Allah’s practice is to send guidance. Ask your listener: do you agree the Ummah declined? Has Allah ever left people without a guide at such a time? That was the time of the promised reformer.

cards.q: Proof 7: His success and steady growth
cards.a: The Quran repeatedly says wrongdoers and fabricators do not succeed. The sign of truth is steady, gradual progress despite opposition — as with the Ahmadiyya Community, which has grown from one man in Qadian to a worldwide community, while false movements flare up and are destroyed.
cards.x:
The Quran says again and again that wrongdoers and those who forge lies against Allah do not prosper (6:22; 10:70; 16:117). Success over time is a test of a claim.

The Promised Messiah (as) received the revelation: “I will carry your message to the ends of the earth.” The Ahmadiyya Community began with one man in Qadian and has grown steadily into a worldwide community, despite severe opposition and persecution.

False movements may flare up for a while, but they do not keep growing for over a century under persecution. Ask which false claimant’s community has done this, then read 6:22.

cards.a: Allah reveals His unseen in abundance only to those He chooses as messengers. The Promised Messiah (as) made a great number of prophecies that were fulfilled, many recorded with witnesses in his book Haqiqat al-Wahi.

cards.q: Proof 9: “And others from among them who have not yet joined them” (62:4) — the man from Persia
cards.a: Surah al-Jumu’ah foretells a second raising of the Holy Prophet (sa) among “others” who have not yet joined the Companions. Asked who they were, he placed his hand on Salman the Persian and said: if faith went up to the Pleiades, men — or a man — from these would bring it back. The Promised Messiah (as) was of Persian descent.
cards.x:
Surah al-Jumu’ah says the Holy Prophet (sa) would be raised among “others from among them who have not yet joined them” (62:4) — a second coming of his message among later people.

When the Companions asked who these people were, the Holy Prophet (sa) put his hand on Salman the Persian and said that even if faith went up to the Pleiades, men — or a man — from these people would bring it back (Bukhari).

Verse 32:6 speaks of an affair rising to Allah over a thousand years. After the first good centuries, faith declined for a long period — bringing us to the time of the promised reformer. The Promised Messiah (as) was of Persian descent, fulfilling the sign of the man from Salman’s people.

cards.q: Proof 10: He came at the head of the 14th century (mujaddid hadith)
cards.a: The Holy Prophet (sa) promised a reformer at the head of every century. The Promised Messiah (as), born 13 February 1835 (14 Shawwal 1250 AH), began receiving divine communication around 1290 AH and made his claim at the head of the 14th century AH — exactly when the Mahdi and Messiah were expected.
cards.x: Many scholars expected the Mahdi around the 13th–14th century AH: Hujaj al-Kiramah (Nawab Siddiq Hasan Khan), Qiyamat-nama (Shah Rafi’uddin), Iqtirab al-Sa’ah (Nawab Nurul Hasan Khan), Maktubat of Mujaddid Alf Thani, and others listed in the Pocket Book. Where is the mujaddid of the 14th century, if not him?

cards.q: Proof 11: The eclipses in Ramadan (Dar Qutni)
cards.a: The Holy Prophet’s descendant Imam Muhammad Baqir narrated that the Mahdi will have two signs never shown since the creation of the heavens and earth: an eclipse of the moon on the first of its eclipse nights in Ramadan, and of the sun in the middle of its eclipse days in the same Ramadan. This happened in 1894 (lunar 13 Ramadan, solar 28 Ramadan 1311 AH), while a claimant to Mahdi-hood was present.
cards.x: The moon is eclipsed only on the 13th, 14th or 15th night of a lunar month, and the sun only on the 27th, 28th or 29th day. The prophecy was fulfilled on 21 March 1894 (13 Ramadan, lunar) and 6 April 1894 (28 Ramadan, solar), visible in the East; it recurred in the West in 1895. The Pocket Book lists scholars who cited this hadith, including Nawab Siddiq Hasan Khan (Hujaj al-Kiramah).

cards.q: Proof 12: His name was Ahmad (61:7)
cards.a: Jesus foretold a messenger named Ahmad. The Holy Prophet (sa) is its first fulfilment; the Promised Messiah’s actual name was Ahmad — “Ghulam” was a family prefix (Ghulam Murtaza, Ghulam Qadir…). His father named two villages Qadirabad and Ahmadabad after his two sons.
cards.x: The verses around it speak of the latter days: “they seek to extinguish Allah’s light” (61:9) and “that He may make it prevail over all religions” (61:10) — the worldwide triumph of Islam that commentators link to the time of the Messiah.

cards.q: Proof 13: Camels abandoned — a sign of his time
cards.a: The Holy Prophet (sa) said in the time of the Messiah young camels would be abandoned and no longer used for travel. The Quran also says “when the she-camels ten months pregnant are abandoned”. The coming of railways and modern transport — including the Hejaz railway towards Makkah and Madinah — fulfilled this in the time of the Promised Messiah (as).
cards.x: Camels were the main means of travel for centuries; the hadith links their abandonment to the Messiah’s time — showing 81:5 also refers to that age.

cards.q: Are the Messiah and the Mahdi two people or one?
cards.a: One. The Holy Prophet (sa) said: “There is no Mahdi except Jesus son of Mary,” and called the coming Jesus “Imam, Mahdi, just arbiter”. When he spoke of the reformer at the end of his Ummah, he named only the Messiah — no separate Mahdi.
cards.x: The idea of two separate persons comes from mixing many weak narrations. The strong ones describe one reformer with two roles: Mahdi (guided Imam) for the Muslims and Messiah (breaker of the cross) facing Christianity.

cards.q: What does “nuzul” (descent) mean in the Quran and Hadith?
cards.a: Nuzul does not mean falling from the sky. The Quran uses “anzala” for iron, clothing, cattle and even the Holy Prophet (sa) himself — all made or born on earth. In hadith it is used for a traveller arriving or settling at a place. A prophet’s “descent” means his honoured coming by Allah’s command.
cards.x:
Many people picture the Messiah’s “nuzul” as falling from the sky. The Quran uses the same root in a different sense. Allah says He “sent down” iron (57:26), clothing (7:27) and even a Messenger — the Holy Prophet (sa) himself (65:11–12). None of these fell from the sky; they were made or born on earth.

In the Hadith, nuzul is used for a traveller stopping at a place, and for a group of the Ummah settling in Basra.

So the descent of a prophet means his honoured coming by Allah’s command. Ask: did iron and cattle fall from the sky? Then why must nuzul mean that for the Messiah?

cards.q: If he is from this Ummah, why is he called “Ibn Maryam”?
cards.a: People are named after others whose qualities they share. The Holy Prophet (sa) called his own wives “companions of Yusuf”. The Promised Messiah (as) resembled Jesus in his circumstances, temperament and mission — a servant-prophet of a great law-giving prophet, appearing in the 14th century after him, as Jesus came about 14 centuries after Moses.
cards.x: We say of a generous man “he is a Hatim”. The Promised Messiah (as) wrote that he resembles the first Messiah in humility, trust in God, signs and nature, “like two pieces of one substance or two fruits of one tree”; and just as Jesus was a follower and servant of the law of Moses, he is a follower and servant of the law of Muhammad (sa).

cards.q: Why can’t Jesus of Nazareth himself be the Messiah of this Ummah?
cards.a: (1) He was a messenger only to the Children of Israel (3:50); (2) the dead do not return (39:43); (3) this Ummah is “the best Ummah” — if it cannot produce its own reformer and must borrow an Israelite prophet, that lowers the Holy Prophet’s (sa) spiritual power.
cards.x: If the Israelite Jesus came as a messenger to the whole world, “a Messenger to the Children of Israel” in the Quran would no longer be true — and the Quran is binding until the Last Day. The hadith “your Imam from among you” confirms the coming one is from this Ummah.

cards.q: The coming Messiah and the Mahdi share the same description
cards.a: The Holy Prophet (sa) described the coming Messiah as wheat-coloured (adam), and the promised Mahdi as wheat-coloured too — while the Israelite Jesus was reddish with curly hair. One description for the Messiah and Mahdi, another for Jesus of Nazareth: two different people, and the Messiah-Mahdi is one.
cards.x:
The Holy Prophet (sa) described three people. Jesus of Nazareth, whom he saw at the Mi’raj, was reddish with curly hair. The coming Messiah was wheat-coloured with straight hair, the most handsome of wheat-coloured men. The Mahdi was also wheat-coloured, of medium build.

Both descriptions of Jesus and the coming Messiah are in Sahih al-Bukhari. Two different descriptions point to two different people. Meanwhile the coming Messiah and the Mahdi share one description.

A simple way to show it: draw two columns — Jesus of Nazareth (reddish, curly hair) and the coming Messiah = Mahdi (wheat-coloured). This supports the hadith “there is no Mahdi except Jesus”: they are one person.

cards.q: “He will be buried with me in my grave” — what does it mean?
cards.a: It cannot be literal: no one may open the Holy Prophet’s (sa) grave. The Quran says Allah “causes every human to die and assigns him a grave” — even those burned or lost at sea — so “grave” can mean a spiritual state. It means the Messiah will be so close to the Prophet (sa) spiritually that they are as one.
cards.x: People whose bodies are burned, eaten by animals or lost at sea still enter the “grave” of the verse (barzakh). So the word is not limited to a physical pit. The hadith points to the Messiah’s complete spiritual union with the Holy Prophet (sa).

cards.q: “At the Mi’raj Jesus said he would descend and kill the Dajjal” — is it authentic?
cards.a: This is a statement of Abdullah ibn Mas’ud (mawquf), not a saying of the Prophet (sa), in Ibn Majah; a narrator (Bundar, Muhammad b. Bashshar) was accused by contemporaries of lying in narrations from Yahya, and Ibn al-Madini rejected one of his reports strongly. It cannot establish a belief.
cards.x: Shah Abdul Aziz Dehlawi (‘Ujala-e-Nafi’a) warns that late narrations unknown to the early generations are not reliable for establishing belief. Also, at the Mi’raj the Prophet (sa) met Jesus among the souls of DEAD prophets, beside Yahya (as).

cards.q: “He will break the cross and kill the swine” — literally?
cards.a: The Messiah’s work is spiritual: to break the doctrine of the cross (prove Jesus did not die an accursed death on it, ending the basis of atonement) and to remove impure behaviour, by arguments and signs. Another version says he will “put an end to war” (yada’ al-harb) — so it cannot mean going around smashing crosses and killing animals.
cards.x: Breaking wooden crosses would not change anyone’s belief; proving that Jesus survived the cross breaks Christianity at its root. “Jizya will be abolished” because religious wars end — the victory is by argument. See the site cards “Breaking of the Cross”, “Killing of the Swine”, “Abolition of Jizya”.

cards.q: Revelation “Anta minni wa ana minka” (You are from Me and I am from you)
cards.a: This is an Arabic idiom of closeness and love, not of being part of God. The Quran and the Holy Prophet (sa) use exactly this phrasing between people; the Promised Messiah (as) himself called it a metaphor (isti’arah).
cards.x: Ibn Khallikan (Wafayat al-A’yan) explains: Arabs say “I am not of so-and-so, nor is he of me” to express distance; and the reverse expresses nearness — as in the Prophet’s (sa) words about Ali. The Promised Messiah (as) explained the revelation as a metaphor (Haqiqat al-Wahi, Ruhani Khaza’in vol. 22). Interpreting a statement in a way its speaker rejects is not fair.

cards.q: Revelation “You are to Me like My son” — isn’t that shirk?
cards.a: The revelation says “bi-manzilati” — LIKE (in the position of) a son, i.e. beloved, not an actual son. The Promised Messiah (as) strongly rejected any idea of God having a son. Scholars like Shah Waliullah explained that “sons of God” in earlier scriptures meant “beloved ones”.
cards.x: Bi-manzilat = in the place/rank of — compare the Prophet (sa) to Ali: “You are to me in the position (bi-manzilat) of Harun to Musa” — Ali was not Harun. A hadith also calls creation “the family of Allah” (al-khalqu ‘iyalullah). Maulana Rahmatullah Kairanawi (Izalat al-Awham) likewise explained “son” in the Bible as a beloved one.

cards.q: Revelations “Kun fa-yakun” and “I’mal ma shi’ta” — claiming God’s power?
cards.a: “Kun fa-yakun” is spoken by Allah about Himself, with “Say” understood before it, as at the start of Surah al-Fatiha. “Do as you wish, for I have forgiven you” means Allah has made His will the servant’s will — his nature now loves only what Allah loves. Saints like Abdul Qadir Jilani recorded similar revelations.
cards.x: The Promised Messiah (as) explained: “Do as you wish” means forbidden things have become hateful to you and good deeds have been placed in your nature — whatever pleases God has become the servant’s own pleasure (Barahin-e-Ahmadiyya part 4). An Arya or Christian could object to the Quran in the same way by taking “kun fa-yakun” out of context.

cards.q: Revelation “Lawlaka lama khalaqtul aflak” (But for you I would not have created the heavens)
cards.a: This was originally said about the Holy Prophet (sa). In every great reformer’s time a new spiritual “heaven and earth” are made — angels are set to serve his mission and hearts on earth are prepared. Iqbal and Mujaddid Alf Thani used the same idea for perfect believers.
cards.x: The Promised Messiah (as): “In the time of every great reformer a new heaven and new earth are created spiritually” (Haqiqat al-Wahi, RK vol. 22). Mujaddid Alf Thani wrote that such people are the security of the people of the earth, through whom rain and provision come (Maktubat). Iqbal: “Mu’min nahin jo sahib-e-laulak nahin” (Bal-e-Jibril).

cards.q: “I saw in a vision that I was God” — what about this?
cards.a: It is a dream/vision, and dreams are interpreted, not taken literally — like Yusuf (as) seeing the sun, moon and stars prostrating to him. Sufis call this state fana fillah: complete absorption in God, where the servant’s own self disappears.
cards.x: He wrote in the same place that this meant nothing of his own remained — everything became God’s — and that he did not believe it in the sense of incarnation (hulul) or pantheism. Holding a person to the literal meaning of a dream they themselves interpreted is unjust.

cards.q: He called himself “Maryam” and spoke of spiritual pregnancy — how?
cards.a: This is the Quran’s own metaphor. Surah al-Tahrim gives Mary as an example for BELIEVERS (men and women): a believer first reaches the “Maryam” state of purity, then Allah breathes His spirit into him and he progresses to the “son of Mary” (Messiah) state. The Promised Messiah (as) described his own spiritual journey in these terms.
cards.x: Zamakhshari explains that “Mary and her son” in the hadith means two TYPES of people — all who have Mary’s or the Messiah’s qualities. So a righteous believer is metaphorically “Maryam”, and through a spiritual “pregnancy” becomes a spiritual “Ibn Maryam”. Words like pregnancy and labour pains in his writings are this same metaphor (Kashti-e-Nuh).

cards.q: The Muhammadi Begum prophecy — was it fulfilled?
cards.a: It was a conditional warning prophecy for relatives who mocked Islam: if Ahmad Beg married his daughter elsewhere, he would die within three years and her husband within two and a half. Ahmad Beg died within six months; the family was frightened and repented, so the husband, Mirza Sultan Muhammad, was spared — exactly as the revelation’s condition “O woman, repent, repent” allowed.
cards.x:
• The family (Ahmad Beg’s circle) mocked the Holy Prophet (sa) and Islam; the prophecy was a sign for them.
• Ahmad Beg died in 1892, within the stated time — the family was struck with fear.
• Mirza Sultan Muhammad never opposed or denied him; he later wrote respectfully of the Promised Messiah (as), and his son joined the Community. The Promised Messiah (as) challenged opponents: get Sultan Muhammad to publish a denial — they could not.
• The precedent: the people of Yunus (as) repented and the punishment was lifted (10:99).

cards.q: Proof 1: All peoples and religions agree that God exists
cards.a: Every religion in history — Islam, Christianity, Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, Zoroastrianism — agrees there is one Supreme Being, even if they differ on His attributes. Even the ruins of extinct civilisations show belief in God. People separated by oceans and centuries could not have agreed on a fabrication.
cards.x:
The first proof is the agreement of mankind. Every major religion — Islam, Christianity, Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism and Zoroastrianism — agrees there is a Supreme Being, even though they differ about His attributes. Even the remains of ancient civilisations show belief in God.

These peoples were separated by oceans and centuries. They could not have met and agreed on a made-up idea. Such universal agreement suggests a truth placed in human nature and taught by messengers to every people.

The Quran points to this continuity: the same teaching was in the earlier scriptures of Abraham and Moses (87:15–20). It is a good starting point because it begins from common ground.

cards.q: Proof 2: The testimony of thousands of truthful people
cards.a: Thousands of the most truthful people in history — the prophets and saints — testified that they spoke with God and He with them. In any court, the witness who says “I saw it” is preferred over the one who says “I did not see it”. The atheist only says he did not see; they said they did.
cards.x: Philosophers taught truthfulness but often did not live it; the prophets lived it under persecution. Their characters guarantee their testimony.

cards.q: Proof 3: Human nature and conscience point to God
cards.a: Every human has an inner sense of right and wrong — the self-reproaching soul (nafs lawwamah) that blames us for lying or cruelty, even in atheists. This moral law inside points to a Law-giver. Man also did not create himself: he grows from a weak, lowly state, so he could not have been his own creator.
cards.x:
Every person has an inner voice that blames them for lying or cruelty — even when no one else knows, and even if they do not believe in God. The Quran calls this the self-accusing soul (75:3). A moral law inside us points to a Law-giver who placed it there.

The second point is about our origin. Man grows from a weak and lowly beginning; he did not make himself. The Quran asks: were they created from nothing, or are they themselves the creators (52:36)?

A simple question opens the discussion: why does your conscience trouble you when you lie, if no one will ever find out?

cards.q: Proof 4: Perfect order in creation — not chance
cards.a: The universe shows flawless harmony and purpose: the giraffe’s long neck, roots for trees, water and sun for the child before it is born. Clever human engineers make mistakes that destroy whole systems — yet “chance” never errs? Design points to a Designer.
cards.x:
The universe shows order and purpose everywhere: the giraffe’s long neck to reach its food, roots to feed the tree, water and sunlight ready for a child even before it is born.

Human engineers, with all their intelligence, still make mistakes that can wreck whole systems. Yet we are asked to believe that blind chance produced a universe without such mistakes. Design points to a Designer.

The Quran invites this test: look at the creation of the Gracious God — do you see any flaw? Look again and again; your sight will come back tired (67:4–5). Use one concrete example, then read the verse.

cards.q: Proof 5: Those who believe in God succeed; those who deny Him fail
cards.a: Every messenger who called people to God faced the fiercest opposition, yet each one triumphed and his opponents were forgotten or disgraced — Ram, Krishna, Moses, Jesus, Muhammad (sa). A powerless man cannot defeat the world alone unless a Living God is with him.

Every messenger who called people to God faced the strongest opposition — Ram, Krishna, Moses, Jesus and Muhammad (sa) among them. Each began alone and powerless, and each one triumphed in the end, while those who opposed them were forgotten or disgraced.

Ask your listener to name one true prophet who failed, or one persecutor of prophets who is honoured today.

cards.q: Atheist objection: “God cannot be seen, so He is imaginary”
cards.a: Many real things are unseen: reason, air, the soul, electricity, time. Even if God were visible, the blind could not see Him. Anything the eye can see must be limited and in one direction; God is beyond limits — being seen would make Him limited, which is a defect.
cards.x: If God were visible to all, faith in the unseen (iman bil-ghayb) and its reward would have no meaning.

cards.q: Atheist objections: differences of religion, rich and poor, sin of believers, “where is God?”
cards.a:
• Different religions: like one doctor giving different medicines to different patients, God gave laws suited to each people; later human changes caused further differences.
• Rich and poor: a king’s palace has a minister and a gardener, yet that does not disprove the king; differences give purpose and test.
• Believers who sin: disobedience does not disprove a ruler — thieves exist in every state.
• Where/since when: time and place are creations; the Creator is not bound by them.
cards.x:
Atheists often raise four objections. Each can be answered with a short example.

Why are there different religions? A doctor gives different medicines to different patients. God gave each people guidance suited to them (13:8), and later human changes added further differences.

Why rich and poor? A king’s palace has a minister and a gardener; their different roles do not disprove the king.

Why do believers sin? Thieves exist in every state, but that does not prove there is no ruler.

Where is God, and since when? Time and place are His creations; the Creator is not bound by them. Answer each point briefly rather than lecturing.

cards.a: No. Jesus called God “my God and your God”, said “my Father is greater than I”, refused even to be called “good” because only God is good, and said eternal life is to know “the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent.” “Son of God” in the Bible is used for Adam, Israel, David, the righteous and peacemakers.

cards.q: Atonement — why it cannot be true
cards.a: Punishing an innocent person for others’ sins is injustice, not mercy; forgiveness that needs a blood price is not forgiveness. Jesus was crucified against his will (he prayed “let this cup pass”), so it was no willing sacrifice. Christians still sin after believing; and the Old Testament teaches that God forgives the one who repents, and that each bears his own sin.
cards.x: The Pocket Book gives some 35 arguments, e.g.: if Jesus bore all sins, he became the sum of sin; the Torah never mentions atonement through a son of God; a judge who hangs the innocent and frees the guilty is unjust. In Islam, a broken oath is expiated by feeding the poor — the sinner pays, not an innocent.

cards.q: Christian objections to the Promised Messiah answered
cards.a:
• “Jesus himself must come from heaven”: Jesus said “ye shall not see me henceforth till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord” — someone coming in his name; and Elijah’s return was fulfilled in John.
• “Many false Christs will come”: a false one is known by failure; he prospered with signs.
• “Punishments should come after the Messiah, not before”: punishment follows rejection of a messenger (17:16).
• “Prophecies failed”: warning prophecies can be withdrawn — Jonah’s 40-day prophecy about Nineveh (Jonah 3:4–10).
• Abdullah Atham: he showed fear and turned towards truth; he refused the sworn challenge with a reward of up to 4,000 rupees.
• “I am a worm of the earth”: David said the same — “I am a worm, and no man” (Psalm 22:6) — humility, not disqualification.
cards.x:
Christians raise several objections against the Promised Messiah (as). Short answers:

Jesus must come himself: Jesus said they would not see him until they said “Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 23:39) — someone coming in his name. Elijah’s return was fulfilled in John.

Many false Christs will come: a false one is known by failure; he prospered and showed signs.

Punishments came before the Messiah: the Quran says punishment follows the sending of a messenger (17:16).

Failed prophecies: warning prophecies can be withdrawn if people turn back, as with Jonah and Nineveh (Jonah 3:4–10). Abdullah Atham showed fear and refused the sworn challenge.

“I am a worm of the earth”: David said the same (Psalm 22:6) — it is humility.

cards.q: Why did the Promised Messiah write harshly about “Yasu”?
cards.a: He distinguished between the Jesus of the Quran — a true, honoured prophet whom he loved — and the imaginary “Yasu” of the Christian missionaries, who abused the Holy Prophet (sa). In reply, he showed what the missionaries’ own Gospel picture implies, without meaning the Quranic Jesus. He wrote that whoever says he does not respect Jesus son of Mary is a mischief-maker and a liar.
cards.x: He claimed likeness to Jesus; if he insulted Jesus he would insult himself. The Quran’s Jesus confirmed earlier prophets and foretold Ahmad (61:7); the missionaries’ Yasu called earlier prophets thieves and robbers (John 10:8) — they are not the same figure.

cards.q: “Jesus was superior to Muhammad (sa)” — miraculous birth, Mary, the cradle
cards.a:
• Born without a father: Adam had neither father nor mother — that does not make him greater (3:60).
• Mary “chosen above the women of the worlds” (3:43): the women of her time; Asiya, Khadija and Fatima are also named among the best women.
• Speaking in the cradle: means speaking wisdom from a young age — the same is said of Yahya (19:13); and “kahlan” shows normal speech.
• Unusual events at birth: the Holy Prophet’s birth also had remarkable signs.
cards.x: The Quran mentions these points about Jesus and Mary to clear them of Jewish accusations, not to raise them above the Holy Prophet (sa).

cards.q: “Jesus was superior” — reviving the dead, creating birds, healing the blind, sinlessness
cards.a:
• Reviving the dead: the Quran uses “dead” for the spiritually dead (6:123); the Holy Prophet (sa) revived a whole nation.
• “I create (akhluqu) for you like birds”: khalq here means to shape/fashion; true creation belongs only to Allah — he trained people to fly spiritually.
• Healing blind and lepers: also spiritual healing, and others healed too.
• Raised to heaven: no verse says an angel took him bodily to heaven.
• Sinlessness: “dhanb” for the Prophet (sa) (48:3) refers to shortcomings attributed by enemies or protection from them, not sin; “dallan” (93:8) means lost in love/searching for his people’s guidance.
cards.x:
Christians — and some Muslims — say Jesus (as) was superior because of his miracles and sinlessness. The Quran explains these differently.

Reviving the dead: the Quran calls the spiritually dead “dead” (6:123), and the Holy Prophet (sa) gave life to a whole nation (8:25). Creating birds: khalq here means shaping; true creation belongs to Allah alone, and false gods cannot create even a fly. Healing: also spiritual, and others healed too. Raised to heaven: no verse says he was taken there bodily.

On sinlessness: dhanb for the Holy Prophet (sa) in 48:3 refers to shortcomings alleged by enemies, and dallan in 93:8 means searching in love for guidance for his people — not sin.

cards.q: “He flattered the British government”
cards.a: His praise was gratitude for religious freedom: under Sikh rule Muslims in the Punjab could not even give the adhan; British rule restored freedom to preach. Islam teaches thanking a just ruler, as the Muslims who migrated to Abyssinia praised the Christian Negus. He gained nothing from the government; and many statements were written to counter opponents who were telling the government he was a rebel “Mahdi”.
cards.x: At the same time he wrote that the British were the Dajjal in their religious aspect, called their Christian “god” dead, and invited Queen Victoria to accept Islam (Tohfa-e-Qaisariyya). A flatterer does not call the ruler’s religion false.

cards.q: Did the Promised Messiah abolish jihad?
cards.a: No. He taught that jihad of the sword is a defensive command with conditions — when Muslims are attacked with the sword for their faith. Since in his age religion was attacked with pen and argument, the jihad of the age is by pen and the Quran (“jihad kabir”). He wrote that the sword-jihad is postponed (not abolished) and would apply again if those conditions return. Ahmadis fought in defensive war, e.g. the Furqan Battalion in Kashmir (1948).
cards.x: Sayyid Ahmad Barelvi, Nawab Siddiq Hasan Khan and other scholars gave the same ruling about fighting the British. Allama Iqbal and Sulaiman Nadvi also wrote that jihad does not mean only fighting. Many scholars who objected never fought either.

cards.q: Prophecies of world wars, earthquakes and the Musleh Mau’ud
cards.a: He foretold great earthquakes and a terrible world catastrophe (fulfilled in the World Wars), and in his announcement of 20 February 1886 he prophesied a son — the Promised Reformer (Musleh Mau’ud) — with some 50 qualities: “He will grow rapidly in stature… will be filled with secular and spiritual knowledge… nations will be blessed through him.” Hazrat Mirza Bashiruddin Mahmud Ahmad, born 12 January 1889, became the second Khalifa (1914–1965) and fulfilled it.
cards.x:
In his announcement of 20 February 1886, the Promised Messiah (as) foretold the birth of a son — the Promised Reformer (Musleh Mau’ud) — and listed many of his qualities: he would grow rapidly, be filled with secular and spiritual knowledge, and nations would be blessed through him.

Hazrat Mirza Bashiruddin Mahmud Ahmad was born on 12 January 1889 and became the second Khalifa, leading the Community from 1914 to 1965. His life is matched against the prophecy point by point.

He also foretold great earthquakes and a terrible world-wide calamity in Haqiqat al-Wahi and Barahin-e-Ahmadiyya part 5. Read the 1886 announcement, then show how the Second Khalifa’s life fulfilled it.

cards.q: Questions for the Lahori (Paighami) Ahmadis on prophethood
cards.a: The Lahoris say the Promised Messiah never claimed to be a prophet. But after 1901 he wrote clearly: “I am a prophet and also an ummati”; “a law-bearing prophet cannot come, but a prophet without law can”; “this gift (of prophethood) opened only through reflection and annihilation in the Messenger.” His last letter (May 1908) repeats he is a prophet according to the hadith.
cards.x:
The Lahori (Paighami) Ahmadis say the Promised Messiah (as) never claimed to be a prophet. His own later writings answer this.

In Ek Ghalati ka Izala (1901) he explained that this gift opened only through complete devotion to the Holy Prophet (sa). In Tajalliyat-e-Ilahiyya he wrote that a prophet with a law cannot come, but one without a new law can. In his last letter (Akhbar-e-Aam, 26 May 1908) he wrote: “I am a prophet and also an ummati,” so that the Holy Prophet’s (sa) prophecy that the Messiah would be both might be fulfilled.

Reading his statements after 1901 settles the question in his own words.

cards.q: How should we test any claimant to be from God?
cards.a: Three ways, all of which the book applies to the Promised Messiah (as): (1) transmitted proofs — what the Quran and Hadith foretold about the time and signs; (2) rational proofs — his life, his teaching, his success and the need of the age; (3) the spiritual way — sincere prayer to Allah for guidance, which He has promised to answer.
cards.x:
Before arguing details, agree on how any claimant should be tested. Tabligh-e-Hidayat gives three ways.

First, transmitted proofs: what the Quran and Hadith foretold about the time and signs of the coming reformer. Second, rational proofs: his life before the claim, his teaching, the need of the age and his success. Third, the spiritual way: sincere prayer to Allah for guidance, which He has promised to answer (29:70).

The Quran also asks claimants and their opponents alike to bring proof (2:112). Agreeing on the method first keeps the conversation fair and focused.

cards.q: Allah sent messengers to every nation — Ahmadis honour the founders of other religions
cards.a: The Quran says every people had a warner. So Ahmadis accept the truth of the prophets of all nations — besides Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, also figures like Zoroaster, Buddha, Krishna and Confucius are respected as possibly sent by God. When the world became connected, Allah sent one universal Messenger, Muhammad (sa), for all mankind.
cards.x:
The Quran says there is no people to whom a warner has not been sent (35:25). So Ahmadis accept that Allah sent guides to every nation, not only to the Israelites.

Besides Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, Ahmadis respect founders such as Zoroaster, Buddha, Krishna and Confucius as possibly sent by God. When the world became connected, Allah sent one universal Messenger, Muhammad (sa), for all mankind (34:29).

This is a strong bridge in conversations with people of other faiths: we honour your founder too, and we invite you to the Messenger sent for everyone.

cards.q: Are the signs of the Messiah to be taken literally?
cards.a: Many signs in prophecies are metaphors, just as earlier prophecies were: the Jews waited for Elijah literally and rejected Jesus. Taking every sign literally creates confusion and contradictions (e.g. the Dajjal’s donkey with ears 70 arm-lengths apart). The right approach: signs that are clearly fulfilled in their spirit, especially those confirmed by events, are the true ones.
cards.x:
Prophecies about the coming of a messenger have often been fulfilled in a spiritual rather than literal way. The Jews waited for Elijah to come down literally and rejected Jesus; Jesus said John the Baptist was Elijah (Matthew 11:14).

Taking every sign of the latter days literally leads to impossible pictures — for example a donkey of the Dajjal with ears seventy arm-spans apart.

The sound approach is to recognise signs fulfilled in their true meaning, especially those confirmed by events. Start with the example of Elijah and John, which both Christians and Muslims can follow.

cards.q: Signs of the Latter Days in Surah al-Takwir — fulfilled in our age
cards.a: Surah al-Takwir lists signs: camels abandoned, seas joined (canals), people brought together, books spread. Our age saw railways, cars, aeroplanes; the Suez and Panama canals; post, telegraph, telephone, radio; the printing press spreading books and newspapers everywhere — exactly the time of the Messiah.
cards.x:
Surah al-Takwir lists signs of a great change in the world: she-camels abandoned, seas made to flow into one another, people brought together, and books spread abroad (81:5–11).

Our age has seen exactly this: railways, cars and aeroplanes replacing the camel; the Suez and Panama canals joining seas; post, telegraph, telephone and radio bringing people together; and the printing press spreading books and newspapers everywhere.

These signs point to the time of the Messiah. Give one modern example for each verse — it is easy for listeners to see for themselves.

cards.q: Who is the Dajjal?
cards.a: The Dajjal (great deceiver) is described with symbols: one-eyed (seeing only the material world), with mountains of bread and rivers of water (vast wealth), riding a donkey that travels fast (modern transport), deceiving the world. These point to the materialist Christian powers and their missionary campaign of the Latter Days, which the Messiah would defeat with arguments.
cards.x: The Prophet (sa) said reciting the first ten verses of Surah al-Kahf protects from the Dajjal (Muslim) — and those verses warn against the doctrine that God has taken a son (18:5). This shows the Dajjal’s fitna is linked to the Christian doctrine.

cards.q: Signs: the state of Muslims, plague and the White Minaret
cards.a:
• Muslims would follow the ways of earlier nations step by step, split into 73 sects, and faith would rise to the Pleiades — until a man of Persian descent brings it back.
• Dabbat al-ard (a creature of the earth) would wound people who reject the signs — the plague of 1897–1907, after which the Community grew from hundreds to hundreds of thousands.
• The Messiah descends at the White Minaret east of Damascus — Qadian lies east of Damascus, and the Minarat al-Masih was built there: a symbol of his light being seen from far.
cards.x:
Several signs of the Messiah’s time are listed together.

The state of Muslims: the Holy Prophet (sa) said Muslims would follow the ways of earlier nations step by step (Bukhari), and faith would rise to the Pleiades until a man of Persian descent brings it back.

The plague: the Quran speaks of a “creature of the earth” that would wound those who reject the signs (27:83). The plague of 1897–1907 is understood as this sign, and the Community grew greatly during it.

The White Minaret: the Messiah descends at the White Minaret east of Damascus (Muslim). Qadian lies east of Damascus, and the Minarat al-Masih was built there as a symbol of his light being seen from afar.

cards.q: “Lam yabqa min al-nubuwwah illal-mubashshirat” — only glad tidings remain?
cards.a: The hadith says nothing of prophethood remains except “mubashshirat” (true visions). This means law-bearing prophethood ended, while its essence — communication from Allah with news of the unseen — continues for the Ummah. A prophet without new law is exactly one who receives abundant mubashshirat.
cards.x:
The hadith in Bukhari says nothing of prophethood remains except mubashshirat — glad tidings, such as true visions.

This means law-bearing prophethood has ended, while its essence — communication from Allah with news of the unseen — continues in the Ummah. The Quran confirms that the friends of Allah receive glad tidings in this life (10:65).

A prophet without a new law is someone who receives such communication in abundance. So the hadith does not close the door; it shows what kind of prophethood remains open. Ask: do true visions still come? Then the essence of prophethood remains.

cards.q: “If there were a prophet after me, it would have been Umar”
cards.a: This hadith means no prophet would come in the Prophet’s (sa) own lifetime or immediately after him, among the Companions; even Umar, with his rank, was not made a prophet. It does not shut the door forever — just as the same Prophet foretold the Messiah who is called “Nabiullah” four times in Sahih Muslim.

Tirmidhi records the hadith: “If there were to be a prophet after me, it would have been Umar.”

cards.q: Does a prophet have to bring a new law? Can a prophet follow another prophet?
cards.a: No. Many prophets brought no new book and followed the Torah: Aaron, Samuel, David, Solomon, Zechariah, Yahya. The Quran says “the prophets who submitted judged by the Torah”. Every prophet is obeyed by his people — but he can himself be a follower of a greater prophet. The Promised Messiah is such a prophet under the Holy Prophet (sa).

cards.q: “There is consensus (ijma’) that no prophet can come” — is that true?
cards.a: No such ijma’ exists. Major scholars — Ibn Arabi, Abdul Wahhab Sha’rani, Mulla Ali Qari, Shah Waliullah, Abdul Hayy Lucknawi, Qasim Nanotwi — wrote that only law-bearing prophethood ended. And everyone who believes Jesus will return as a prophet already accepts a prophet after the Holy Prophet (sa).
cards.x:
Opponents say there is ijma’ (consensus) that no prophet of any kind can come. No such consensus exists.

Major scholars wrote that only law-bearing prophethood ended: Ibn Arabi, Abdul Wahhab Sha’rani (Al-Yawaqit wal-Jawahir), Mulla Ali Qari, Shah Waliullah, Abdul Hayy Lucknawi and Qasim Nanotwi among them.

Moreover, everyone who believes that Jesus (as) will return as a prophet already accepts a prophet after the Holy Prophet (sa). Ask: do you believe Jesus will come as a prophet? Then there is no consensus that no prophet can come.
