cards.q: Are Men and Women Equal in Islam? Answer Hazrat Khalifatul Masih I (RA)
cards.a:
The Holy Qur’an teaches that all believers, without distinction, are equal, and that a person is elevated only through righteousness. However, Islam also recognises that equality does not mean that men and women are identical. Men and women have different physical and emotional strengths, and in view of these differences, Islam assigns them different roles and responsibilities in life.

The roles are therefore not a question of superiority or inferiority, but a question of natural capacity and proper functioning. For example, men have been assigned the duty to work and provide for their family and women have been assigned the role of motherhood and of looking after the household.

Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets; and Allah has full knowledge of all things.

Sunni Muslims interpret the above verse to mean that Muhammad (S.A.W) is the last prophet, and they often allege that Ahmadi Muslims deny this verse of the Holy Quran because they believed in a prophet after him (S.A.W). cards.q: Khala (خلا) & Khalat (خلت) in Arabic Lexicons & Dictionaries
cards.a:
Khalā (خلا) means to pass away. In the context of a human passing away, it only means the following:

It is never used to describe flying physically towards heaven.

Classical Arabic lexicographers are unanimous on the root Kh-L-W (خ-ل-و). When this verb is used in reference to past human generations, leaders, or messengers, it denotes their passing away from the realm of the living into death.

Whoever asserts that the Arabic verb Khalā (خلا) or its feminine form Khalat (خَلَتْ) signifies flying physically into heaven while remaining alive carries the entire burden of proof. There is zero entry in any classical or modern Arabic dictionary that supports such an interpretation.

cards.q: Fosterage and Childhood — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 1
cards.a:
It was a custom among the nobles of Makkah that mothers did not suckle their own children. Instead, children were normally sent outside the city and were entrusted to Bedouin wet nurses. The obvious benefits of this were that infants would remain vigorously healthy and grow strong as a result of the pure and unpolluted rural environment. Moreover, they would learn to speak excellent precise Arabic.

Initially the young Muḥammadsa was suckled by his mother and later
Thuwaibah also nourished him with her milk. Thuwaibah was a slave-girl who belonged to Abū Lahab, the paternal uncle of Muḥammadsa. Abū Lahab freed her at the birth of his orphan nephew as an expression of his gratitude. It was this very Thuwaibah who suckled Ḥaḍrat Ḥamzahra as well. Hence, Ḥamzahra, who was the uncle of Muḥammadsa, also became his foster brother through the relationship of milk.

cards.q: Introduction — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 3
cards.a: At this point, the question naturally arises: how was it possible that there were no clouds and the Holy Prophetsa prayed and clouds appeared and it began to rain? Then, when this rain became excessive the Holy Prophetsa prayed that the rain be withheld and the clouds dispersed and the horizon cleared. cards.q: Sanctity of the Ka‘bah — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 1
cards.a: In the time of the Jāhiliyyah the Arabs held the Ka‘bah in greater reverence than perhaps the Muslims of today. It was because, the Arabs viewed the Ka‘bah as a deity to be worshipped and would offer oblations to it. These offerings would be stored in an underground treasury and would be utilised for the requirements of its worshippers and pilgrims. The Ka‘bah in itself was of course sacred, but through it, not only Makkah, but its surrounding regions were also declared a Haram where all kinds of violence and bloodshed was prohibited. The significance of the Ashhur-e-Ḥurum was also due to the Ka‘bah, so that pilgrims could travel to and fro for the Ḥajj in complete peace without any fear or danger. cards.q: Construction of the Ka‘bah — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 1
cards.a:
Following this secondary yet necessary discussion, we now return to our actual subject matter. It has already been mentioned that under Divine command, Abrahamas brought Hagaras and her infant child to settle in the desolate valley of Makkah after which he returned home. When Abrahamas visited Makkah for the second and third time, Hagaras had passed away.
Coincidentally, Ishmaelas was also absent, due to which a reunion of father and son could not take place. cards.q: Ancient Religions of Arabia — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 1
cards.a:
Prior to Islām, Arabia was composed of the followers of many diverse religions – the most distinctive of which were Idolatry, Atheism, Zoroastrianism,
Sabianism, Christianity and Judaism. Of these religions the most common and wide-spread throughout the country was the religion of idolatry, which in actuality, should be referred to as the true religion of the country. Idolaters did acknowledge the existence of Allāh the Exalted, but considered their idols a means to reach Him. They were entangled in their intermediary mediators to such an extent as the thought of their true creator had escaped their minds. In addition to commonly shared idols, every tribe possessed its own exclusive idol as well. In Makkah, Isāf and Nā’ilah were the idols of the Quraish, before which sacrifices were slaughtered. ‘Uzzā was an idol situated in Nakhlah, commonly shared by the Quraish and Banū Kinānah.

Among the foul habits of the Arabs, three were particularly distinct.
Drinking, gambling and fornication were so abundantly rampant that may

cards.q: Arabian Trade and Commerce — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 1
cards.a: The national professions of the Arabs were three alone: firstly, agriculture, which was confined to a significantly small portion of the entire country, secondly, to nourish and maintain cattle, which is more commonly known as pasturing, and thirdly, trade and commerce, which should be considered the largest profession in Arabia. Since time immemorial the people of Arabia were professionals in commerce. Tribes which were settled near the coast or lived near civilised countries were diligently engaged in trade since the ancient times. In the early era, it was primarily the Arabs who imported and exported goods between the east and the west. Therefore, their mercantile caravans would travel regularly between Syria and Egypt on one side and along the coasts of the Indian Sea on the other. This consistent travel served as a connecting commercial chain between Syria, Egypt and India.

cards.q: Arabian Civilization Prior to the Advent of Islam — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 1
cards.a:
Prior to the advent of Islām, the country of Arabia, with the exception of a few coastal regions, was in a state of complete isolation from the outside world. So much so, as no outside nation or sovereignty ever cast an impression upon it, nor did the people of Arabia ever leave their homeland permanently.
Prior to Islām, a civilised or centralised sovereignty within the country was never established. Although upon certain instances various governments were established in some regions, their authoritative jurisdiction was applicable only at the local level. The country never bowed before a single ruler; rather, every tribe was free and had its own particular chieftain. However, in Arabia, no one actually received leadership by inheritance, nor was it in the form of an established sovereignty.

cards.q: Climate — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 1
cards.a:
Geographers acknowledge the fact that external winds can reach
Arabia from two directions alone: the north-east and south-west. However, there exists nothing but dry land on both sides; therefore, the winds that enter
Arabia are naturally dry and devoid of moisture. It is for this very reason that there is a dearth of rain in the country. However, mountainous regions still extract the little moisture that these incoming winds bring, and due to this fact, some rainfall does occur in these regions as well. The passing of the Tropic of Cancer through the centre of this country also contributes to its desert condition and shortage of water. To geographers it is not hidden that a region of this type, with regards to constant winds, is a zone of placidity. Therefore, it must be generally stated that Arabia is an arid country.

cards.q: Topography — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 1
cards.a:
In regards to topographical land characteristics, geographers have categorized Arabia into three types. First is the coastal region which extends over uniformly levelled surface, and in contrast to other regions, is temperate.
Second is the mountainous region with valleys, which are the heart of the country. Third is the wilderness, which due to its vast desert, is usually barren and uninhabited.
Along the western coast of Arabia, a range of mountains runs north and south, known as Jabalus-Sarāt. Some of the mountains of this range reach an altitude of 8,000, or rather 10,000 feet, but the total average altitude is quite minimal. From the centre of this range, another series of mountains, which in actuality is a combination of many smaller mountainous regions, is spread extensively to the north and south.

cards.q: Formation and Land Area — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 1
cards.a:
The formation of Arabia is of an irregularly shaped rectangle surrounded by water at three of its boundaries, and land at its fourth one.
The Arabian coastline is very small, in proportion to its girth, which naturally results in a lack of fine sea-ports.
The area of Arabia is approximately 1.2 Million square miles and it is approximately 1,600 miles long and 700 miles wide. Hence, in reference to its area, Arabia is among the large countries of the world. However, if one analyses its population, various smaller countries appear larger in comparison. At present, the total population of Arabia is no greater than 8 Million. The cause of this shall become apparent ahead.

cards.q: Fundamental Perspective on Islamic Equality — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 3
cards.a:
The essence and summary of the Islāmic philosophy on equality is comprised in a few Qur’ānic verses and Aḥādīth. Allāh the Exalted states in the Holy
Qur’ān:

“O Ye People! fear your Lord in mutual affairs. Fear him who created you from a single soul, wherefrom He created its mate. And from them twain spread many men and women.” 1

In this Qur’ānic verse, Allāh the Exalted has led the attention of man to the eternal truth that they are the children of a single father, and the branches of a single tree, and has established the foundation of true equality in the world. Moreover, He has also informed us of the principle that irrespective of the difference which may come about between various peoples and classes as a result of circumstances, in mutual relations they should never overlook the fact that in their origin they are the progeny of a common forefather.

One aspect of the science mentioned last in the above mentioned list is also referred to as Magāzī. cards.q: Prohibition of Alcohol — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 2
cards.a:
Section: VIII – Blow of a Misfortune, Law of Inheritance, Prohibition of Alcohol, Treachery of the Disbelievers and Two Tragic Incidents

It has already been mentioned that alcohol was consumed heavily in Arabia. As a matter of fact, drinking had become a part of the national characteristics of the Arabs. No gathering was deemed complete without alcohol. As a matter of fact, among particular types of people, special times had been appointed when they would gather and intoxicate themselves. Due to his purity in nature, although the Holy Prophetsa had never consumed alcohol himself, and abstained from this ill-habit even prior to his prophethood, and various Companions had also refrained from its usage from the very beginning, until then, since alcohol had not been forbidden religiously, many people from among the Companions would drink.

cards.q: Principles of Riwayat & Dirayat — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 1
cards.a:
The fundamental principles of this knowledge are that the integrity of every instance can be tested on the basis of two methods, and unless its

authenticity is evidently established by both methods, one cannot vest full confidence in it. The first method is of Riwāyat. In other words, the objective is to test the external testimonies of the instance which has been narrated.
Hence the purpose is to determine whether the channel through which the narration has reached us is adequately reliable or not. The second method is of
Dirāyat. In other words, the objective is to put to trial the internal testimonies of the instance that has been narrated. That is, irrespective of the channel through which the narration has reached us, whether the instance in itself and on the basis of its environment, can be presumed to be true and authentic.

This is because the Holy Prophetsa was one to prefer seclusion from the beginning and never intermingled with the common society of Makkah during any part of his life. cards.q: A Paucity of Narrations — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 1

Now the first era of the life of the Holy Prophetsa has come to an end.
Yet a sense of contentment is missing and the heart does not let the hand stop writing. It appears as if the events of the first 40 years of the life of the Holy
Prophetsa are not preserved with such details as were the events of the latter era. This is very natural because the way he was looked upon in the time of his prophethood, was missing in that first period. Still, had early historians exerted more attention on the period of life prior to prophethood and had sought events with greater diligence and effort, many additional details could have been found. cards.q: Luminosity of Dawn — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 1

Muḥammadsa had now reached the ripe age of 40 years. The time had come for the light of dawn to manifest itself upon the Eastern horizon.
Muḥammadsa never intermingled with the general society of Makkah. For he was one who desired solitude and during this time, his disposition was such as day and night, he would remain in seclusion longing for Allāh the Exalted, diligently occupied in his remembrance. At a distance of three miles from
Makkah towards Minā, in the left is the mountain of Ḥirā, wherein is a cave, famously known as the Cave of Ḥirā. During this time, it was the general practice of Muḥammadsa to retreat to this cave and would occupy himself in deep meditation and rememberance of God. Ordinarily, he would take sufficient food with him and would not return to Makkah for many days.

cards.q: Arrival at Madinah and the First Friday Prayer — Seal of the Prophets Vol. 2
cards.a:
Section: I – Early Establishment of Madinah and Foundation of the Islamic Government

The Holy Prophetsa was perhaps still in Qubā’ when the Muslims of
Madīnah began to discuss whose home the Holy Prophetsa would stay at.
Every family desired the honour of hosting the Holy Prophetsa. When the

It was when, not only the invention of printing was yet to come into existence, but also, the art of writing and composition was still in its preliminary stages of development. Based on the famous Christian calendar system, the time period of the Holy Prophetsa is stated to be from
570 A.D. to 632 A.D. It is that period in time when a majority of the nations of the world were absolutely unacquainted with the art of composition and it was prevalent to some extent in such nations who, in one form or another, were advanced politically or literally. However, as shall soon become apparent, prior to Islām not only was Arabia entirely isolated from the outside world, it was also completely devoid of every kind of educational, political and social movement internally as well.

Upon the third degree are the internal narrations of the Arabs themselves and in reality, these very narrations serve as a solid base in the study of Pre-Islāmic history. The art of writing and composition was not prevalent among the Arabs, but the method in place for the preservation of verbal narrations from generation to generation was very common. For this purpose the Arabs were gifted with an exceptional memory – the likeness of which cannot be found in any other nation. A distinctive class existed in every tribe, which was responsible for safeguarding to memory the historical account of their own tribe as well as that of surrounding tribes with integrity and loyalty of the highest calibre. Among the Arabs, this art was known as ‘Ilmul-
Ansāb, meaning, ‘The Science of Genealogy’. In history, the names of many have been recorded from the Pre-Islāmic era, as experts in this art.

Sabr [Patience] is one of the natural human states. One has to exercise it in the face of calamities, ailments and hardships which constantly befall him. The same is the case with the soul. When a person moves away from God,

The first of these is when you are warned that you are about to be afflicted with a calamity. For instance, imagine that a warrant has been issued for your presence in court. cards.q: Repentance Washes Out the Stains of Sin — Essence of Islam Vol. 2
cards.a: Though God Almighty has announced that the seed of the Unity of God is present in every soul, He has also expounded that that seed is not in equal strength in everyone and that the natures of some are overcome to such a degree by their passions that that light almost disappears. It is obvious, therefore, that the innateness of animal or aggressive faculties is not inconsistent with the innateness of belief in One God. However much a person may be given to following his desires, and however much he might yield to his evil-directing self, he possesses to some degree a natural light. For instance, if under the impact of passion or anger a person commits theft, murder, or adultery then though this act of his is a demand of his nature, yet the light of well-doing which is invested in his nature rebukes him at the very time when he indulges in any of these improper activities.

A persevering and goodnatured supplicant smells the perfume of the favours of his Lord in these trials and difficulties and his intelligence informs him that they will be followed by help.
One aspect of these trials is that they foster eagerness for prayer. The greater the distress of the supplicant, the more his soul will be melted. This is one of the factors in the acceptance of prayer. So one should not lose heart and should not think ill of God through impatience and restlessness. cards.q: Is religion to blame for violence in the world? (Introduction)
cards.a:
Hazrat Mirza Tahir Ahmad (rh) explains why he wrote this book. It began in the late 1950s in Urdu as Mazhab ke Nam par Khoon (Bloodshed in the Name of Religion), after the violent anti-Ahmadiyya riots of 1953 in Pakistan.

The riots were over, but the questions they raised were not: Is Islam a religion of war or of peace? Does it allow persecution, looting or murder over differences of belief? The book answers these questions from the Quran and the life of the Holy Prophet (sa), and shows that violence in the name of Islam has no basis in its teaching.

cards.q: What is the "Maududian law of apostasy" and why is it wrong?

The Quran, by contrast, says: “whoever wishes may take the way that leads to his Lord” (76:30).

cards.q: Is there such a thing as "Islamic terrorism"?

cards.q: Did Hazrat Abu Bakr (ra) fight apostates for leaving Islam? (the Siddiqi era)

Supporters of the death penalty point to Hazrat Abu Bakr (ra) and call it “Siddiqi Sunnah”. Huzoor (rh) shows this is not what history records.

cards.q: The narrations of killing a female apostate and of the eras of Umar (ra) and Ali (ra) — examined
cards.a:
Maududi cites the killing of a woman named Umm Qirfa. Huzoor (rh) shows she was killed for constantly inciting her thirty sons to make war on the Muslims, not for apostasy — and her sons were spared.

He also examines a narration of Ikrimah used to support killing apostates, and quotes early authorities who doubted Ikrimah’s reliability. And he cites a hadith in Nasa’i that names, among the cases where killing is allowed, an apostate who takes up arms against Allah and His Messenger — showing the issue is fighting, not belief.

cards.g: The Truth about the Alleged Punishment for Apostasy in Islam
cards.q: Does "qatl" (killing) in these narrations have a figurative meaning?
cards.a:
In Arabic, qatl (killing) is often used figuratively. Lexicons such as Taj al-Arus and Lisan al-Arab note phrases like “he killed the matter” (he understood it fully) and “he killed the wine” (he diluted it). The Quran uses qutila to mean “cursed be”.

In a hadith, a person at prayer is told to “kill” someone passing in front of him — meaning to stop him. Huzoor (rh) shows that some narrations about “killing” — for example about anyone who seeks leadership — were never acted on literally. So the word “kill” in such narrations need not mean execution.

cards.g: The Truth about the Alleged Punishment for Apostasy in Islam
cards.q: Which hadith refute the death penalty for apostasy?
cards.a:
Several hadith show the Holy Prophet (sa) did not kill apostates.

A Bedouin pledged allegiance, fell ill in Madinah and three times asked the Prophet (sa) to cancel his Islam. He refused, and the man left Madinah. The Prophet (sa) only said: “Madinah is like a furnace that removes impurities” (Bukhari) — he did not order him killed. An apostate who hid with Hazrat Uthman (ra) was forgiven (Abu Dawud). And Hazrat Umar (ra) said that apostates should be offered return, and if they refused, put in prison — not killed (Kanz al-Ummal).

cards.g: The Truth about the Alleged Punishment for Apostasy in Islam
cards.q: Is there an ijma (consensus) of early scholars on killing apostates?
cards.a:
Supporters of the death penalty claim ijma — consensus. Huzoor (rh) shows there was none.

In Abu Bakr’s (ra) time, captured apostates were not killed, and no Companion objected that the law required their death — itself a silent consensus against it. Later authorities also disagreed: Fath al-Qadir says an apostate is killed only to remove the danger of war, not for disbelief; al-Sarkhasi says a female apostate is not killed; and Ibrahim Nakha’i said an apostate should be given respite until his natural death. With such opinions, no consensus can be claimed.

cards.g: The Truth about the Alleged Punishment for Apostasy in Islam
cards.q: What do present-day ulema say about apostasy, and why are they so rigid?
cards.a:
Present-day scholars also disagree. Imam Mahmud Shaltut, former rector of al-Azhar, wrote that the Quran only says apostates’ works are lost and they face punishment in the Hereafter; that fixed punishments (hudud) cannot rest on a single-chain hadith; and that killing is allowed only against those who fight Muslims.

Huzoor (rh) then examines why some ulema are so rigid. He argues that enemies of Islam welcome the death penalty for apostasy because it makes Muslims destroy each other, while weak Muslim governments would never apply it to Hindus, Christians or Jews.

cards.g: The Truth about the Alleged Punishment for Apostasy in Islam
cards.q: Were earlier prophets themselves accused of apostasy?
cards.a:
The Quran gives a long history of the prophets and their opponents. It shows that the enemies of every prophet believed that anyone who left the ancestral religion must be punished severely.

Noah, Abraham, Salih, Shu’aib and Moses were all accused of apostasy and threatened with punishment, and Allah sided with His prophets and condemned their enemies. So, says Huzoor (rh), if there is any consensus on punishing apostates, it is the consensus of the enemies of the prophets — not of the prophets or their true followers.

cards.q: The Pakistan government's reasoning against Ahmadis on apostasy — and the reply
cards.a:
Huzoor (rh) replies to the Pakistan government, in the words Moses used against Pharaoh: “I seek refuge in my Lord from every arrogant person who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning” (40:28).

He points out that even the Holy Prophet (sa) was accused by his people of leaving their faith and turning others away from it. It is a deep tragedy, he says, that today it is people who claim to follow the Holy Prophet (sa) who demand death for apostasy, while other faiths that once held this belief have abandoned it. He ends by asking for prayers for all suffering people.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: How did Christianity move from facts to fiction? (Introduction)
cards.a:
Hazrat Mirza Tahir Ahmad (rh) explains his approach. Jesus (as) matters to Christians, Jews and Muslims alike, and if they could agree about him, many of the world’s problems would ease. But arguing from scriptures alone has produced two thousand years of disagreement.

So he chooses logic and reason as common ground. He also notes how the Church long resisted scientific discovery (for example Galileo), and how, as knowledge spread, the clash between Christian dogma and reason led many Christians to stop taking their beliefs seriously.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: Can Jesus (as) be the literal Son of God? (science of parenthood, virgin birth, miracles)
cards.a:
Can Jesus (as) be the literal Son of God? In ancient times, when people did not understand how a child is born, it seemed possible for a god to have a son. Science now shows that a child receives equal chromosomes from mother and father.

Huzoor (rh) asks what “literal son” can then mean for Jesus, who had a human mother and no human father. He also discusses virgin birth in nature (parthenogenesis) and explains that miracles are laws of God beyond our present knowledge, not breaks in His laws. A virgin birth does not make anyone divine.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: Does the doctrine of sin and atonement make sense? Did Adam's sin pass to all mankind?
cards.a:
Orthodox Christianity teaches three things: God is just and cannot forgive without punishment; all humans inherit Adam’s sin; and only a sinless person can atone for others — so Jesus had to die for mankind.

Huzoor (rh) examines each part. Sin is not inherited like a gene. Human suffering and death continued after the crucifixion, so the punishment was not removed. And a few days of suffering cannot pay for the sins of countless people — like paying a debt of trillions with one penny. Jesus’ true, lovable life has been turned into a strange myth.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: Can justice and forgiveness both be served by Jesus' sacrifice? Who was really sacrificed?
cards.a:
The Christian doctrine of atonement assumes God cannot simply forgive, because justice and forgiveness cannot go together. Yet the New Testament itself teaches forgiveness more strongly than any other scripture — “turn the other cheek”. If the Son taught forgiveness, why could the Father not forgive?

Huzoor (rh) also asks whether the sacrifice was willing: in Gethsemane Jesus prayed three times for the cup to pass from him. He concludes that there is no evidence the doctrine of atonement came from anything Jesus (as) said, did or taught.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: Did God the Father suffer too? Was limited suffering enough for unlimited sin?
cards.a:
If God the Father and the Son are of one substance, how could the Son suffer in hell for three days while the Father felt nothing? Either the Father suffered too, or the Unity of God is broken and there are separate gods.

Huzoor (rh) also asks why death should be such an agony for a divine being, and why, if he truly died, he would return to the same body. And if the Son showed more noble suffering than the Father, does that mean divinity is still developing? These questions show the doctrine does not hold together.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: What is the role of the Holy Ghost — mystery or paradox?
cards.a:
The Holy Ghost is said to be a distinct person, yet fused with the Father and the Son into one. Huzoor (rh) asks whether the three have separate egos — separate “I”s. If they do, they are three beings; if they do not, they cannot be three persons.

He also asks what role the Son and the Holy Ghost play in creation and in running the universe. If they are passive partners, they are inferior to the Father. Christians are told to believe without understanding — but such faith cannot be offered to a non-believer as reasonable.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: Did Jesus (as) die on the cross? The sign of Jonah and the events of the crucifixion
cards.a:
The Ahmadiyya view is that the crucifixion was an attempt to murder Jesus (as) that failed. After a few hours on the cross he was taken down in a deep swoon, before death, and later recovered.

Huzoor (rh) examines the Gospel accounts: Pilate’s surprise that he was “already dead” (Mark 15:44), the body being handed over to Joseph of Arimathea, and Jesus’ own sign of Jonah — alive in, alive out. God answered his prayers in Gethsemane by saving him from an accursed death.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: Revival or resurrection: what happened to Jesus' body after the cross?
cards.a:
If Jesus (as) truly died, medical science says his brain would have begun to decay within minutes. Returning to life after three days would mean the soul coming back to a dead brain — something that raises serious problems.

Huzoor (rh) also discusses the harsh language some Jewish sources used against Jesus, and the question of the empty tomb. The simple answer, he says, is that Jesus had not died. He recovered, met his disciples in his physical body, and then left Judea, as he had promised, to find the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: What is the Ahmadiyya view of the crucifixion, and do people survive crucifixion?
cards.a:
The Ahmadiyya view is clear: Jesus (as) suffered on the cross, was delivered by God as he had prayed, and then migrated in search of the ten lost tribes of Israel, fulfilling his mission to all the tribes.

The Promised Messiah (as) declared this about a hundred years ago. Huzoor (rh) also gives modern cases of people declared dead who revived — for example a man in Bengal in 1909 — and medical studies of near-death experiences. Seeing someone lose consciousness and later seeing him alive does not prove he rose from the dead.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: Does the Trinity hold together logically?
cards.a:
Why three persons in God? Huzoor (rh) quotes Christian scholars such as Harnack and Rev. K. E. Kirk, who admit that the early writers gave no reason for a third person — the question for them was simply “why not?”

He examines possible ways of understanding three persons — as phases of one person, as persons sharing eternity, or as persons with different or identical characters — and shows that each runs into contradiction. Jesus (as) worshipped the Father and asked others to do so; he never asked anyone to worship himself or the Holy Ghost.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: How did Christianity evolve after Jesus (as)? The role of St Paul
cards.a:
The doctrine of the Trinity did not exist in Jesus’ (as) lifetime. It took centuries to form, through bitter debates and under the influence of the cultures where Christianity spread.

The first followers of Jesus were Jews who had learned directly from him. Huzoor (rh) shows how they were divided over his nature and over keeping the Law, and how St Paul turned Christianity in a new direction towards the Gentiles. He then traces the reality of Jesus as a prophet in the line of Israelite prophets, and Islam as the final stage of religious development.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: Christianity today: colonialism and the expected return of Jesus
cards.a:
The biggest problem of Christianity today, says Huzoor (rh), is not lack of understanding but lack of will to accept the truth. Christianity has become part of Western civilisation and served its colonial and economic power more than its spiritual purpose.

He then turns to the expected return of Jesus. If Jesus is expected to descend bodily from the sky, people who live by such legends may never recognise their redeemer when he actually comes — as a human child, like every prophet before him.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: Who is the Promised Messiah that Christians are waiting for?
cards.a:
Just over a hundred years ago, Hazrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (as) of Qadian was told by God that Jesus of Nazareth was a special prophet who died like all other prophets, and was never lifted bodily to heaven. The promised second coming, awaited by Christians and Muslims alike, was to be spiritual, not literal — and God had raised him to fulfil it.

Huzoor (rh) describes how his Community spread worldwide, though still small compared with the Christian world, and invites Christians to consider his claim.

cards.g: Christianity: A Journey from Facts to Fiction
cards.q: Conclusion: Christianity — a journey from facts to fiction
cards.a:
Huzoor (rh) closes with an appeal to Christians to come down from the “ivory tower of make-believe” to the realities of life. Jesus (as) was a perfect man for his age, a special messenger of God given the title of Messiah — but no more than a man.

He compares the Jews, who waited for Elijah to descend from heaven and rejected Jesus, with those today who wait for Jesus to descend and reject the Messiah who has come — Hazrat Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (as).

cards.q: Introduction: what happened to Jesus (as) after the crucifixion?
cards.a:
This booklet records a question-and-answer session held in March 1982 at Dunyapur, near Multan, chaired by Hazrat Mirza Tahir Ahmad (rh), with non-Ahmadi guests asking about the death of Jesus (as).

He began by explaining the basic difference: Ahmadis believe the promised Messiah has already come, while others wait for Jesus to descend bodily from the sky. cards.q: Is Jesus Christ still alive, or did he die?
cards.a:
If the Quran, the Hadith or established facts prove that Jesus (as) is alive, then Ahmadiyyat dies, because its basis is his death. But if the Quran, the Hadith, the Christian scriptures and history all show that he died like other prophets, the whole idea of his bodily ascent and return must be reconsidered.

Huzoor (rh) then begins with the verses of Surah al-Nisa, explaining them in their context: the Jews’ claim that they killed the Messiah, and the calumny they uttered against Mary.

cards.q: Does the Bible support doubt about the death of Christ on the cross?
cards.a:
Yes — the Bible itself shows that Jesus’ death on the cross was doubtful. He was taken down after about three hours, while crucifixion normally killed slowly over days through pain, hunger and exposure. Events were arranged so the sentence came late on Friday, with the Sabbath following.

When his side was pierced, blood and water came out — which does not happen with a dead body. He was not buried in the ground with the two criminals but laid separately in a tomb.

cards.q: Is there other proof besides doubt that Jesus survived?
cards.a:
There is more than doubt. Avicenna’s medical book Al-Qanun mentions an ointment called Marham-e-Isa (the ointment of Jesus), linked to the twelve apostles. Its ingredients heal wounds and stop bleeding — no one uses these on a dead body.

After the crucifixion, Jesus (as) hid from the Jews and met his disciples secretly. Mary Magdalene and the disciples saw him in person, and some were frightened, thinking he was a spirit. He showed his wounds and ate food — the signs of a living man.

What does “rafa’ahullahu ilaihi” in 4:159 mean? Huzoor (rh) explains the Quran by the Quran. The same expression is used for the Prophet Idris (19:58), where it means raising in rank.

Huzoor (rh) quotes a hadith in Kanz al-Ummal: those of the Holy Prophet’s (sa) followers who bow and humble themselves before Allah will be raised to the seventh heaven.

cards.q: What is meant by "ilaihi" (to Himself) in the verse of raising?
cards.a:
Between the two prostrations, Muslims pray: “O Allah, forgive me… and raise me (warfa’ni).” No one asks to be lifted bodily into the sky in the middle of prayer; it means “exalt me spiritually”.

So when Allah says He raised Jesus “to Himself” (ilaihi), it means nearness to Allah and spiritual exaltation. Allah is not in one direction or place, so being raised to Him cannot mean being carried to a physical location.

cards.q: Which Quran verse definitely proves that Jesus died?
cards.a:
Verse 3:145 settles it: “Muhammad is only a Messenger; all messengers have passed away before him. If he dies or is slain, will you turn back on your heels?”

The verse explains “passed away” as dying or being slain — no third way such as bodily ascent. When the Holy Prophet (sa) died, Hazrat Umar (ra) at first refused to accept it, until Abu Bakr (ra) recited this verse. All the Companions accepted that every earlier messenger, including Jesus, had died.

cards.q: What does "nuzul" (descent) mean in the hadith?
cards.a:
The verse 3:145 also refuted Hazrat Umar’s (ra) idea that the Holy Prophet (sa) had gone up to heaven. It proves that no earlier prophet, including Jesus (as), is alive in the heavens.

cards.q: Did anyone witness Jesus' burial? Where is his tomb?
cards.a:
No hadith, history or Gospel records an eyewitness saying Jesus (as) died on the cross, or was dead when taken down or placed in the tomb. Palestinian tombs were large rooms cut into rock, where a wounded man could be cared for; Joseph of Arimathea took the body from Pilate.

cards.q: Is there a tomb of that period in Kashmir, and traces of Christianity there?
cards.a:

He explains that the government had made rejection of the Promised Messiah (as) a matter of law: every citizen was forced either to slander him or lose certain rights. This was not a popular movement but a law imposed from above on ordinary Pakistanis, most of whom had previously taken little interest in Ahmadis.

cards.q: What is the Ahmadiyya philosophy of the revival of religion?
cards.a:
The Ahmadi philosophy of revival is the one common to all religions and supported by history. Scriptures mention people ascending to heaven, but never anyone returning bodily after a long absence. Reformers have always come from ordinary human beings, and have been rejected and persecuted.

cards.q: What was the Holy Prophet's (sa) view on justice?
cards.a:
The Holy Prophet (sa) was strictly just, but his justice was joined with kindness. After Badr, his uncle Abbas was among the prisoners, tied so tightly that he groaned all night. cards.q: Does any religion have a monopoly of truth? Is Islam a universal religion?
cards.a: No Monopoly of Truth While speaking on the subject of the distinctive features of Islam, the first and most attractive feature that strikes one, is its most endearing disclaimer that Islam denies having a monopoly of truth, and that there have been no other true religions. Nor does it claim that Arabs alone have been the recipients of God’s love. Islam is the only religion that totally rejects the notion that truth is the monopoly of any single faith, race or people; instead it professes that Divine guidance is a general bounty that has sustained humanity in all ages. The Holy Quran tells us that there is neither a race nor a people, who have not been blessed with the bounty of Divine guidance, and there is neither a region of the earth nor a body of people who have not received Prophets and Messengers of God.1

When a person truly believes “there is no God but Allah”, false fears and hopes vanish. Without this belief, the human mind and society begin to decline.

cards.q: What does Islam teach about life after death?
cards.a:
Religions that believe in life after death are of two kinds: those that believe in reincarnation and those that believe in another world. Islam rejects reincarnation.

cards.q: Why is there no peace in the world, and what can Islam contribute?
cards.a:
Absence of Peace The single most important malady of the world today is the absence of peace. In the contemporary world, man, as a whole, has reached a high standard of achievement in material progress, made possible by the advancement of science and technology in every sphere of human requirement at a mind-boggling pace.

No doubt, the more fortunate sections of human society, known as the First and Second World, have a much larger share of the fruits of scientific progress in the contemporary age, but the Third World has also benefited to a degree. Rays of progress have penetrated even the innermost recesses of the darkest areas, where a section of human society still lives in a remote past.

cards.q: Are all prophets equal? Does Islam accept prophets of other religions?
cards.a:
Religious Values Have Become Redundant Examining the overall religious scenario, one cannot fail to notice that in religion there seems to prevail a paradoxical situation today. In general, religion is losing its grip yet simultaneously tightening it in different areas. In some sections of society, in almost all religions, there seems to be a powerful swing back in the direction of dogmas with medieval rigidity and intolerance of opposition.

On the moral side, religion is on the retreat; crime is rampant; truth is disappearing fast; equity and the deliverance of justice are on the verge of extinction; social responsibilities to the society are being ignored; and a selfish individualism is gaining strength in its stead even in such countries of the world as would otherwise claim to be religious. These and many other social evils, which are positive signs of a morally decadent society, have become the order of the day.

cards.q: Can salvation be monopolised by one religion? Harmony among religions
cards.a:
Salvation Cannot Be Monopolised by Any Single Religion The question of salvation, howsoever innocent it may appear, is potent in its danger to peace in the religious world.

It is one thing for a religion to declare that those who seek to be redeemed from Satan and attain salvation should rush to the safe haven of that religion; it is there that they would find salvation and eternal liberation from sin. But it is quite another thing for the same religion to declare in the next breath that those who do not come hither to seek refuge will be damned eternally, one and all. Whatever they do to please God, however much they love their Creator and His creation, however much they lead a life of purity and piety, they would most certainly be condemned to an everlasting Fire.

cards.q: Is Islam a universal religion?
cards.a: Islam Is a Universal Religion The Holy Quran repeatedly makes it clear that Islam is a religion whose teachings are related to the human psyche. Islam emphasises that any religion, which is rooted in the human psyche, transcends time and space. The human psyche is unchangeable. Therefore, the religion which is truly rooted in the human psyche becomes unchangeable by the same token provided that it does not get too involved with the transient situations of man, in whatever age, as he Inter-Religious Peace progresses forward. If the religion sticks to those principles, which emanate from the human psyche, such a religion has the logical potential of becoming a universal religion.

cards.q: No compulsion in religion; freedom of speech
cards.a:
Instruments of Struggle—No Compulsion How can a religion claim itself to be universal, international, or global and yet not cause frictions? No religion with a universal message and global ambitions to unite mankind under one flag can even momentarily entertain the idea of employing force to spread its message.

Swords can win territories but not hearts.

Force can bend heads but not minds.

Islam does not permit the use of force as an instrument for the spread of its Message. It declares:

There should be no compulsion in religion. Surely, right has become distinct from wrong;30

cards.q: What does Islam say about blasphemy?
cards.a:
Blasphemy Islam goes one step further than any other religion in granting man the freedom of speech and expression. Blasphemy is condemned on moral and ethical grounds, no doubt, but no physical punishment is prescribed for blasphemy in Islam despite the commonly held view in the contemporary world.

Having studied the Holy Quran extensively and repeatedly with deep concentration, I have failed to find a single verse which declares blasphemy to be a crime punishable by man.

Although the Holy Quran very strongly discourages indecent behaviour and indecent talk, or the hurting of the sensitivity of others, with or without rhyme or reason, Islam does not advocate the punishment of blasphemy in this world nor vests such authority in anyone.

cards.q: What is wrong with today's materialistic social order?
cards.a: Contemporary Social Order Unfortunately religious influence on moral behaviour is fast being lost in society. To aggravate the situation further, a strong urge for liberation from religious obligations is in motion and gaining momentum almost everywhere in the contemporary world. Yet, there is also panic borne out of the growing lack of security and disorderliness in social behaviour running parallel to the trends to disregard religious and ethical codes. Belief in a living God, Who has shaped not only the destiny of human beings but Who also has a right to determine the patterns of their day to day life is rapidly eroding.

cards.q: What are the fundamentals of an Islamic society? Chastity and segregation
cards.a:
Islamic Social Climate Islam, on the other hand, designs to create a climate, which is as different from the one described above, as spring is from autumn.

Within the Islamic concept of society, Islam moderates, disciplines and trims natural desires which, if left uncontrolled, would play havoc with the gamut of human emotions. It discourages or prohibits the fulfilment of desires which can, in the final analysis; result in more misery than pleasure in the society.

At the same time, Islam cultivates new tastes and develops the ability to derive pleasure and satisfaction from acts which may appear colourless, insipid and tasteless to the uncultured and untrained.

cards.q: What rights did Islam give women? Are women equal in Islam?
cards.a:
The Dawn of a New Age in Women’s Rights It is only fitting here to focus our attention to that dark period of time in the history of Arabia when Islam came to be born, through Divine instructions, as we Muslims believe, or as the personal teachings of Muhammadsa, as the non-Muslims would have it. Whatever the view of some theologians, Islamic teachings regarding the segregation of sexes did not represent Arab behaviour at all.

The society in Arabia at that time was extremely paradoxical in its attitude towards women. On the one hand, sexual permissiveness, the free mixing of men and women and mad orgies of wine, women and song were the highlights of Arab society. On the other hand, the birth of a girl was considered to be a matter of disgrace and extreme shame.

cards.q: Why does Islam allow polygamy?
cards.a:
Polygamy In the West it is quite common to confront a speaker on the subject of Islam with the question: does Islam permit one to marry four times and keep four wives simultaneously? I have had vast experience in addressing many public and select gatherings of intellectuals in the Western world. Seldom do I remember an occasion when this question was not raised.

More often than not a lady would stand up, and, of course, with due apologies, innocently enquire whether Islam permits four wives or not. Obviously, everybody knows the answer. But, perhaps, this is the only aspect of Islam which is so widely known in the West. The other well-known aspect is terrorism, but terrorism has nothing to do with Islam.25

Care of the Aged The responsibility for care of the aged is gradually shifting to the state.

Care of the aged represents a heavy burden on the national economy.

However much a state is ready to spend, it can never buy them peace and contentment. The most terrible feeling of having been rejected, left out and abandoned, and the most painful realisation of a growing void of loneliness within, are problems beyond the reach of many to resolve. cards.q: Trust, eradicating evil and do's and don'ts of an Islamic society
cards.a:
Eradication of Evil—A Collective Responsibility The responsibility of educating people is not entrusted to governments but collectively to the people themselves to do good deeds and to abstain from evil.

In more developed societies, it is the job of refuse collectors to gather unwanted waste from homes and streets for disposal. In poorer countries, the housewives simply throw away the junk and refuse on to the streets till the streets become littered with filth and are no longer fit as passageways. Of course it is the responsibility of the inmates to clean the houses but there has to be some system of keeping the streets and pathways clean.

cards.q: Why are drinking and gambling prohibited in Islam?
cards.a:
Prohibition of Drinking and Gambling When one talks of addiction, generally, drugs come to mind. There is another connotation of addiction in a wider sense, which is seldom associated with the word addiction. I refer to society’s regard for Socio-economic Peace certain modes of pleasure, namely drinking and gambling, neither of which augurs well for the peace and good of society.

Gambling is institutionalised in almost all advanced countries of the world. But even in some Third World countries, where it is not institutionalised on such a large scale, gambling is found almost at every level as a small-time individual occupation. Drinking is the second addiction to which societies of the world have fallen prey.

cards.q: Capitalism, communism and the Islamic economic system
cards.a:
Capitalism, Communism and Islam The Islamic economic order neither belongs to capitalism nor to scientific socialism. The economic philosophy of Islam is scientific without being mechanical. It is disciplined without being overrestrictive. It allows private possession and private enterprise but does not promote greed and the amassing of wealth in a few hands whereby a large section of society turns into destitute, serfs and slaves to a cruel and relentless system of exploitation.

There are three fundamental differences in the economic philosophies of capitalism, communism and Islam.

O ye who believe! Surely, many of the priests and monks devour the wealth of men by false means and turn men away from the way of Allah. cards.q: Which political system does Islam prefer? Monarchy and democracy

Political Peace Has to Be Carefully Examined at the National and International Level As far as national politics is concerned, the foremost issue is which political system is good or bad for man. Again, we need to discover whether it is the failure of political systems and their inherent defects which are responsible for the miseries and dissatisfaction of a people or is it something else. Is the system to be blamed or those who run it?

Can immoral selfish, greedy, or corrupt political leadership which rises to power by democratic means be really good and beneficial for society as against benign dictatorship, for instance?

cards.q: What is a true "Islamic government"? Mullahism and divided loyalties
cards.a:
Divine Authority Absolute sovereignty belongs to God. The Holy Quran sums up His domain in the following verse:

Political Peace Then exalted be Allah, the True King. There is no god but He, the Lord of the Glorious Throne.8

The fundamental principle, that ultimately all rights to govern belong to God and He is the Lord of Sovereignty, is mentioned in different ways in the Holy Quran of which the above verse is but one example.

In the running of political affairs, God’s sovereignty is expressed in two ways:
1. The Law (shariah) as derived from the Holy Quran, the conduct of the Holy Prophetsa of Islam and also from the established traditions attributed to him by early Muslims are supreme. They bear essential guidelines for legislation and no democratically elected government can interfere with the express Will of God.
2. No legislative process would be valid in contradiction of the aforesaid principle.

cards.q: How can a person be at peace with himself?
cards.a:
Vying with One Another in Good Deeds According to Islam, both desires and ambitions are activated and curtailed under Divine guidance so that a perfect balance is achieved.

Without such a balance, it is impossible to achieve social peace. Islam promotes such desires and ambitions as are largely independent of one’s financial state of affairs and are available to individuals at all levels at no or nominal cost.

The ambition to rise above the common run of people, and to attain distinction is but natural. However, this natural desire to excel and rise above others, if left undisciplined and uncurtailed can become unwholesome. Jealousy and foul play, for instance, can poison the spirit of free competition to a degree that the entire society begins to suffer rather than benefit from the advantages of a competitive spirit.

cards.q: The three creative principles: justice, benevolence and kinship (Prologue)
cards.a:
Prologue When I woke up this morning and proceeded towards the mosque for prayers, I noticed that the sky was overcast, threatening rain. I thereupon examined my inner thoughts; there was no trace of ingratitude in relation to God for bringing this rain upon us at such an inopportune moment. It was the day of the Annual Gathering (Jalsah) and it seemed that if it were to rain heavily, the Jalsah proceedings would be completely disturbed.
'All praise belongs to Allah' was the spontaneous response of my heart because I found not a flimsiest trace of ingratitude anywhere in the recesses of my heart. At this very moment I was moved to send Darud (salutations) to Prophet Muhammadsa, who is the greatest benefactor of mankind. The Quran cultivates among us the attitude of total submission to the will of God.

cards.q: What does the Quran say about the creation of the universe?
cards.a:
The Creation of the Universe We will now see how all constituent parts of the universe work according to the principles mentioned in the following verse of the Holy Quran:

And the heaven He has raised high and set up the measure, that you may not exceed the measure. So weigh all things with justice and fall not short of the measure.
(Surah al-Rahman; Ch.55: Vs.8-10)

In these verses, God says that He has created the heavens high, pointing out its loftiness as well as its grandeur. Both of these characteristics depend totally upon balance; this celestial universe is not only made on the principle of justice but also works as a touchstone for it.

cards.q: How is the doctrine of Trinity a violation of justice?
cards.a:
Violations of Justice If someone investigates with an open mind the root cause of all evils, whether social, political, economic or moral, he will always find it to be injustice. The world cannot become an abode of peace until man adheres to justice. When injustice, tyranny and oppression take hold, evil is born and destruction is let loose.

If man is not just in his obligations to God, then it is quite unlikely that he will be just to his fellow human beings. It must be remembered that no one can trifle with the dictates of justice without exposing himself to the danger of falling victim to the punishing consequences. Such punishment is not related to the wrath of God as if descended from heaven, but is a natural outcome of the violation of the laws of nature. None is above the dominion of natural laws.

Islam and the Advanced Era of Prophet Muhammadsa We now turn our attention towards the age of the revelation of the Holy Quran. This is the time when, according to the Quran, the development of religion reached its pinnacle and the teachings reached perfection. The Quran says:

cards.q: Justice, benevolence and kinship; the philosophy of prayer
cards.a:
Prayer is the cornerstone of all other forms of worship and it is also modelled according to the three principles of absolute justice, benevolence and kinship. Justice is found in the following Quranic teaching:

And when My servants ask you about Me, say: 'I am near. I answer the prayer of the supplicant when he prays to Me. So they should hearken to Me and believe in Me, that they may follow the right way.' (Surah al-Baqarah; Ch.2: V.187)

Along with the glad tidings (that Allah is near the sincere worshipper)
the Quran mentions the relationship of justice that is established between God and man. Prayer is not a one way street. The worshipper cannot treat God like a slave who stands ever ready to obey his master! Rather, the worshipper should also himself submit to God and obey His Absolute Justice, Kindness and Kinship— Part II commands.

cards.q: What is the evidence for the existence of God?
cards.a: The Testimony of God, His Angels and Knowledgeable People To begin with, the Holy Quran lays the utmost importance on the testimony of God Himself regarding His own existence. Does He or does He not exist? This is that fundamental upon which every religion is based. The question is, if God exists, who saw Him and who bore witness that he has as good as seen Him? It is vital that God Himself should speak of His own existence and present those witnesses who have heard His word. Incidentally, this is another matter which distinguishes the Holy Quran from other Divine books. Many such books fail to present a clear-cut claim made by God Himself that 'I Exist'.

cards.a: REPARE NOw to undertake a journey upon the wings the nature and identity of the jinn. The Quranic concept of jinn has been briefly discussed before in Life in the Perspective of Quranic Revelations. Arabic lexicon mentions the following as the possible meanings of the word jinn. It literally means anything which has the connotation of concealment, invisibility, seclusion and remoteness. It also has the connotation of thick shades and dark shadows. That is why the word 'jannah' (from the same root word) is employed by the Quran to denote paradise, which would be full of thick, heavily shaded gardens. The word jinn is also applicable to snakes which habitually remain hidden from common view and live a life secluded from other animals in rock crevices and earthen holes. It is also applied to women who observe segregation and to such chieftains as keep their distance from the common people. The inhabitants of remote, inaccessible mountains are likewise referred to as jinn.

OR A GAME OF CHANCE!
'The Ball no question makes of Ayes and Noes But Here or There as strikes the Player goes; And He that toss'd you down into the Field, He knows about it all - HE knows - HE knows!'' cards.q: Organic systems and evolution
cards.a:
N ORGAN, in medical terms, is defined as any differentiated part devoted to a specific function.

There are many organs in the human body which need to be studied in-depth to determine whether they evolved gradually over a very long period of time, or were created spontaneously in their finished form as some of the clergy believe. They defy the evolutionary theory of Darwin in its specifics, yet, we insist here that they do not defy evolution itself.

It is a complete misunderstanding on the part of the naturalists that the divide between them and the creationists is the real contention. The religious clergy they often allude to is the extremist faction among the Christian scholars who deny evolution at all levels and believe in spontaneity instead. Spontaneity means that each animal was created separately in its finished form with all the organs it contains. This is certainly not the Quranic concept of creation which we have been explaining throughout the book.

The need for another prophet after the advent of the last is an intrinsically contradictory belief. Yet, the absoluteness of his finality would remain intact as long as the new need is fulfilled by an old prophet. But anyone should be able to see through this transparent effort at cheating. For the sake of the unfamiliar non-Muslim reader we need to explain the historical background of this issue lest they should fail to understand what the row is all about. cards.q: Epilogue: Revelation, Rationality, Knowledge and Truth
cards.a:
EPILOGUE 'N THE END, we turn to the issue of non-prophetic phenomenon of non-prophetic revelation should also come to an end with the ending of prophethood.

Continuity of Divine revelation is indispensable for supporting a profound unshakeable belief in God which cannot be attained with the help of rational investigation alone. Hence, revelation must always play a major role in strengthening belief in the existence of an Omniscient, Omnipotent God.

cards.q: What do Ahmadis believe about Khatam an-Nabiyyin? (Majalis-e-Irfan)
cards.a: Ahmadis believe the Holy Prophet (sa) is Khatam an-Nabiyyin in every true sense of the word: the best and highest of all prophets, the seal whose word is authority, and the last law-bearer — no law will come after his and no one can change his Shariah until the Day of Judgement. What Ahmadis reject is only the meaning that every kind of prophethood, even a follower-prophet, is closed.
cards.x:
A non-Ahmadi lady asked this at the very first Majlis-e-Irfan in Karachi (27 February 1983). Huzoor (rh) first quoted the definition in Pakistan's constitution — that no prophet of any kind, follower or not, can ever come — and said this is the modern ulema's translation, not ours.

He then gave the Holy Prophet's (sa) own usage. He said he was Khatam an-Nabiyyin even when Adam was still being created — so khatam cannot simply mean "last in time". And he told Hazrat Ali (ra): "I am the khatam of the prophets and you are the khatam of the saints" — no one says sainthood ended with Ali.

Arabs used khatam for the best: Mutanabbi was "khatam al-shu'ara", Avicenna "khatam al-atibba". The verse 4:70 shows that perfect obedience to the Holy Prophet (sa) leads to the four ranks: prophet, truthful, martyr, righteous. Scholars such as Ibn Arabi, Shah Waliullah, Mulla Ali Qari and Qasim Nanotwi held that only law-bearing prophethood ended. Hazrat Aisha (ra) said: "Say he is Khatam an-Nabiyyin, but do not say there is no prophet after him." And the Holy Prophet (sa) called the coming Messiah "Nabiullah" four times in Sahih Muslim, and said: "Had my son Ibrahim lived, he would have been a truthful prophet."

cards.q: Why do Ahmadis call their Khalifa "Huzoor" and show him so much respect?
cards.a: No one loves and honours the Holy Prophet (sa) more than the Ahmadiyya Jama'at — read the Promised Messiah's (as) poems in his praise. Respect for others must stay within the manner the Holy Prophet (sa) taught: the Companions stood up for him and for the Khulafa. True respect for him is obedience to him.
cards.x:
A guest asked: the Holy Prophet (sa) did not let Muslims honour him excessively, so how can you accept being called "Huzoor" and "our leader"? Huzoor (rh) answered that no Ahmadi can even imagine giving anyone more honour than the Holy Prophet (sa), and pointed to the Promised Messiah's (as) na'ts as proof of this love.

He said the way of showing respect is the one the Holy Prophet (sa) taught: the Companions stood up when he came, and also for the Khulafa and other elders — but they did not stand up for someone's name in his absence. When asked why Muslims should not show respect in other ways too, he said: of course respect him — but in his way. Leaving his way in the name of respect is really disrespect, because respect means obedience.

cards.q: "We believe the signs of the Imam Mahdi have not appeared yet."
cards.a: The signs before his coming were fulfilled long ago: faith gone, mosques full but empty of guidance, Islam only in name, the Quran only in writing. The ulema themselves announced the Mahdi would come at the head of the 14th century — and when the century passed they had no Mahdi and no Mujaddid. Above all, the sign of the eclipses in Ramadan was fulfilled in 1894, after the Promised Messiah's (as) claim.
cards.x:
Huzoor (rh) said the signs are of two kinds: before his coming and after it. The signs before — the decline of faith, sects, abandoned prayer, Islam in name only — have been visible for over a hundred years; even Akbar Allahabadi wrote about them.

The ulema used to say from every pulpit that the Mahdi would come at the head of the 14th century; Khwaja Hasan Nizami wrote that the signs were complete. When the century passed and no one else claimed, they began saying it was a mistake. But the hadith that a Mujaddid comes at the head of every century is accepted by all — so where did the 14th-century Mujaddid go? Rejecting the Mahdi made them lose the Mujaddid as well.

The clearest sign is in Dar Qutni: the moon eclipsed on the first of its eclipse nights (the 13th) and the sun on the middle of its days (the 28th), in Ramadan, with a claimant present — something that never happened before. It happened in 1894, five years after the Jama'at was founded in 1889. The objection that it should be "the first night of the month" fails, because the Holy Prophet (sa) said qamar (moon), and the moon of the first nights is called hilal.

cards.q: "There is an empty place next to the Holy Prophet's (sa) grave where Jesus will be buried."
cards.a: First, there is no empty place: ask the Saudi government's endowments department. Second, the hadith does not say "next to my grave" but "yudfanu ma'i fi qabri" — he will be buried with me, in my grave. No Muslim would dig open the Holy Prophet's (sa) grave, so the meaning must be spiritual: the Messiah's beginning and end will be one with the Holy Prophet's (sa).
cards.x:
Huzoor (rh) also pointed out a practical problem: if this burial is a sign of the true Messiah, then people will say they will believe only after he dies and is buried there — so no one could ever believe in him in his lifetime.

In Urdu and Punjabi there is an idiom: "you will be buried with me" means "our end will be the same". The Holy Prophet (sa) said of the coming Imam that his name would be like his and his father's name like his father's, and that he would be buried in his grave — meaning their beginning and their end are one. Taking it literally would mean opening the Holy Prophet's (sa) grave, which no Muslim with any honour could accept.

cards.q: Was the Holy Prophet (sa) affected by magic, as some narrations say?
cards.a: No. The Ahmadiyya position is clear: the Holy Prophet (sa) was completely free from the effect of magic. Allah saved Moses (as) from Pharaoh's magicians; the Holy Prophet (sa), far greater, could not be bewitched. What actually happened was that the Jews poisoned his food, which affected his health and memory for a while, and the Jews then spread the story that their magic had worked.
cards.x:
Huzoor (rh) explained that such narrations entered Muslim books through the mischief of some Jews, and gave Christians and others ground for strong objections. Allah promised to protect the Holy Prophet (sa), and his enemies saw this: Abu Jahl, asked why he obeyed the Prophet (sa) at once in a dispute, said he saw two fierce camels beside him.

The Jews poisoned him, and its effect on his health and memory lingered for a while. Meanwhile they threw charms into a well and later claimed that their magic had overcome him. The prophets, he said, are beyond the reach of the world's magicians. For the Khatam an-Nabiyyin the question of magic does not even arise.

cards.q: "If I recite the Kalima, why won't Ahmadis lead or join my funeral prayer?"
cards.a: Every Muslim sect has given the same fatwa against others: your prayer is not valid behind us, ours not behind you. It is a question within Islam, of "kufr less than kufr". Ahmadis do not call other Muslims non-Muslim; but they believe that whoever rejects the Imam sent by God cannot be followed in prayer — exactly what you yourselves will say when your Mahdi comes.
cards.x:
Huzoor (rh) said that in all Ahmadi literature you will never find other Muslims called "non-Muslim"; the term used is "non-Ahmadi Muslim". Funeral prayers and praying behind someone are matters of imamate, and all the sects of the world have issued such fatwas against one another.

He gave the logical conclusion: if the Imam that the Holy Prophet (sa) foretold has come, then praying behind those who deny him is not allowed. Non-Ahmadis say the same about their own expected Imam. But prayer (du'a) for anyone is not forbidden; Ahmadis pray for all mankind, Muslim or not, and share in others' joys and sorrows.

cards.a: The first person ever stopped from Hajj was the Holy Prophet (sa) himself, at Hudaybiyyah. Allah accepted that unperformed Hajj above every Hajj — Surah al-Fath records the reward. Hajj is obligatory only when the way is safe; Allah rewards obedience, not forcing one's way in. Ahmadis are prevented by governments, yet many Ahmadis from around the world do perform Hajj.

cards.q: What are jinn? Do Ahmadis deny them?
cards.a: Ahmadis do not say there is no creation called jinn. The word jinn (from "hidden") is used in the Quran and Hadith both for a separate hidden creation and, in other places, for people — for example powerful, hidden or mountain peoples. The meaning depends on the context.
cards.x:
Huzoor (rh) gave examples. The Holy Prophet (sa) said not to clean oneself with bones because they are the food of jinn — today we know bones carry bacteria that cause infection: a hidden creation. In Arabic, jinn is used even for a snake that hides.

The Quran uses jinn for the strong peoples under Hazrat Sulaiman (as), who were "bound in chains" — something that cannot apply to beings of fire. In Surah al-Rahman, "O company of jinn and men" addresses great powers and common people; and in Surah al-Nas, the whispering comes "from among the jinn and the people" — both groups of people. So an Ahmadi who says jinn do not exist at all is wrong; one who says the word is also used for humans is right.

cards.q: The Quran mentions sihr (magic) — why don't Ahmadis believe in magic?
cards.a: Ahmadis accept magic exactly as the Quran describes it: the magicians of Pharaoh "bewitched the eyes of the people" so that ropes looked like snakes. In modern terms that is mesmerism — deceiving the eye while reality stays the same. What Ahmadis reject is charms and spells (tona-totka), which the Quran never supports.
cards.x: Huzoor (rh) said the Jama'at follows the meaning the Quran itself gives. In the contest with Moses (as), the magicians threw their ropes, and the Quran says they cast a spell on people's eyes and terrified them; the ropes only appeared to move. That is the reality of magic in the Quran. No Ahmadi denies this kind of magic; but there is no Quranic proof for amulets and spells, so they are not accepted.
cards.pg: Majalis-e-Irfan, pp. 65–66

cards.q: "When did you start to feel that Mirza Sahib was the Mahdi?"
cards.a: The Mahdi is not made by feelings. The Mahdi is the one whom Allah clearly appoints and tells "I make you the Imam" — and then supports. Every true claimant is beaten and opposed from the day of his claim, yet God's help makes him grow. Many have claimed to be the Mahdi and vanished; the Promised Messiah's (as) community grew after every attempt to crush it — in 1934, 1953 and 1974.
cards.x:
Huzoor (rh) compared the question to someone who heard the whole story of Zulaikha and then asked whether Zulaikha was a man or a woman. The point is not people's feelings but God's appointment and God's support.

Out of the 124,000 prophets, name one whose claim did not bring persecution. A liar is quickly wiped out, but God's chosen one keeps growing, his followers keep increasing despite killings and looting. He recalled a student at the Australian National University in Canberra who accepted, after discussion, that Jesus (as) had died and asked who the Messiah then was.

When the Holy Prophet (sa) received his first revelation, Waraqa bin Naufal told him his people would expel him. The same happened to the Promised Messiah (as): the day he said God had spoken to him, his people turned against him, calling him dajjal and issuing fatwas of death. Both the opposition and the survival are proofs of his truth.
cards.pg: Majalis-e-Irfan, pp. 66–71

cards.q: Can another prophet come? And how can the Imam Mahdi be a prophet if the Holy Prophet (sa) is Khatam an-Nabiyyin?
cards.a: A follower-prophet (ummati nabi) can come — but only one whose coming the Holy Prophet (sa) himself foretold. How many will come is the Holy Prophet's (sa) decision, not ours. He foretold the Mahdi and called the coming Messiah "Nabiullah" four times; so accepting him as a prophet in that sense does not contradict Khatam an-Nabiyyin.
cards.x:
Huzoor (rh) explained that in the Quran a prophet and the Imam Mahdi have the same meaning: one whom Allah appoints by revelation and whose acceptance He makes obligatory. Logically, perfect obedience to the Holy Prophet (sa) can lead to follower-prophethood; but in fact only those whom he foretold will come, because he is the Messenger until the Day of Judgement.

If tomorrow someone else claims, the Jama'at will ask him to show the Holy Prophet's (sa) glad tidings about him; without his authority, no one can be accepted. The very one in whose honour the verse of Khatam was revealed foretold a coming "Nabiullah" — so in that sense accepting him as prophet is unavoidable, and is not against the verse.
cards.pg: Majalis-e-Irfan, pp. 71–74

cards.q: "Your prayer and fasting are like ours — so why were you declared kafir?"
cards.a: The 1974 decision of Pakistan's National Assembly deserves examination. It was an assembly of politicians of every type — some who never prayed, some who took bribes — deciding who is a Muslim. It was claimed that the Ahmadi belief about Khatam an-Nabiyyin is so different that they lose the right to be called Muslims. Yet Ahmadis believe the Holy Prophet (sa) is Khatam an-Nabiyyin; the Imam Mahdi's rank as a follower-prophet does not contradict it.
cards.x:
Huzoor (rh) said he was present in the Assembly in 1974 with Hazrat Khalifatul Masih III (rh) and four other members of the Jama'at. The world was only told that Pakistan's representative Assembly and great ulema had given a verdict; he explained what the reality was.

The basis given was the belief about Khatam an-Nabiyyin. He explained the Jama'at's firm belief: the Holy Prophet (sa) is the seal of the prophets, his Shariah final; the Mahdi he foretold is his follower and his prophet only through obedience to him. That cannot be the basis of declaring anyone outside Islam.
cards.pg: Majalis-e-Irfan, pp. 75–81

cards.q: Why is it necessary to believe in the Imam Mahdi?
cards.a: All the scholars of the Ummah agree that it is necessary to accept the Imam Mahdi, and that whoever rejects him becomes a kafir. Ahmadis hold exactly the same belief about Hazrat Mirza Sahib that other Muslims hold about the Mahdi they await — the only difference is that we say he has come.
cards.x:
Huzoor (rh) suggested asking the ulema two questions about the expected Mahdi: will Allah appoint him by revelation, or will he be elected? And will his rejecters be called kafir? Their answer will be: Allah will appoint him, and whoever rejects him will be a kafir.

That is precisely the definition of a prophet: someone God appoints and whose acceptance He makes obligatory — the Quran gives no such example for a non-prophet. So the ulema who accuse Ahmadis of denying Khatam an-Nabiyyin hold the same belief about their own Mahdi. If such a belief took Ahmadis out of the Ummah, it would take them out too. The Quran also says Allah made Imams "who guide by Our command" (21:74) — the Mahdi is one who is first guided, then guides.
cards.pg: Majalis-e-Irfan, pp. 82–87

cards.q: "The Promised Messiah's (as) language in his books doesn't sound like a prophet's."
cards.a: The objection comes from reading books of opponents with fabricated or mistranslated quotations. The harsh words he used were not abuse: they were written in debates with Christians who were insulting the Holy Prophet (sa) and his wives, to show them how it hurts. Out of more than eighty books, only a few sentences are picked out of context and posted on leaflets.
cards.x:
Huzoor (rh) said: if she had read the original books, she would know he never wrote such things about any Muslim. Where hard words appear, they answer the Christian missionaries who attacked the Holy Prophet (sa) and the Mothers of the Faithful. Since Muslims believe in all prophets, he could not answer back against prophets; so he used facts about their own society to make them feel the pain they were causing.

Stating a fact is not abuse. The Quran itself uses strong language for the character of a people — calling some "like apes and swine" and "utul ba'da dhalika zanim" (68:14). No one calls that abuse. When a nation's condition must be shown, strong words are sometimes necessary for the sake of reform.
cards.pg: Majalis-e-Irfan, pp. 91–95

cards.q: "Why is there such a gulf between Ahmadis and other Muslims?"
cards.a: The basic difference is this: the Imam everyone was waiting for — we say he has come. In religious history, when the expected one comes, most of his people do not recognise him, because he looks like an ordinary man, not the grand figure they imagined. Otherwise the Shariah, the Sunnah, the Hadith and the basic beliefs are the same.
cards.x:
A guest said Ahmadi women had good character and followed the Shariah — so why the gulf? Huzoor (rh) said the difference is the concept of how an Imam comes. People expect a Mahdi welcomed with red carpets, garlands and celebrations in mosques; but every true reformer in history was rejected, abused and called a liar, even by his own family.

He called this one of the great tragedies of religious history, repeated with every messenger. Families who accept the Messiah are thrown out of their homes, sons beaten by fathers — and that is the real gulf. Otherwise, he said, the Shariah is the same, the Sunnah the same, the Hadith the same, the deeds the same.
cards.pg: Majalis-e-Irfan, pp. 96–106
